item.title: Four months after Rafael: the Corpus Christi channel log, and the reviews still open
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Two closures, one partial reopening, one full sweep. The port is working normally, and the review of port security is one of several still under way.
item.content:encoded:
Port condition, Corpus Christi, Tuesday: open to all traffic. Four months to the day after Hurricane Rafael's landfall, Gulfwater sets down the log.

Sept. 11 to Sept. 13. Port Conditions X-Ray, Yankee and Zulu in three days. Ships at the offshore anchorage put to sea. Two laden tankers stay at an Inner Harbor berth with Coast Guard approval.

Sept. 14. Landfall near Port Aransas. Oil is reported at the Inner Harbor terminal. The Unified Command later estimates about 9,000 barrels from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay.

Oct. 14. Partial reopening. Spill decontamination restricts the inner channel and a backlog builds at the anchorage.

Oct. 28. Inner-channel restrictions are lifted. The same day, an explosion beside the tug Corrin Bay closes the entrance.

Nov. 5. Navy teams render a second device safe.

Nov. 11. The channel reopens after a 14-day closure and full sweep.

Dec. 28. The Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issue a maritime cyber advisory on vendor remote access to cargo systems.

Jan. 4. U.S. officials attribute the intrusion into the tankers' cargo systems and the channel devices to a foreign government they do not name.

What is open. Reviews of port security, among others, are under way. The FBI investigation continues. The Coast Guard has not released findings from the tanker investigation.

"The channel is open and the port condition is normal," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. She declined to discuss the security review.

"We are part of that review and we welcome it," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "We would rather be asked hard questions now than in September."

What the log shows. The storm closed the port for a month. The entrance closed it for two more weeks. Neither was an ordinary heavy-weather event, and plans written for ordinary ones did not cover them.

Gulfwater will continue to report port condition as it changes, and findings as they are released.

item.title: Inner Harbor spill: about 4,200 damage claims filed as bay fishing grounds partly reopen
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: State agencies reopened part of the closed waters after testing. The claims count gives the first public measure of the spill's commercial reach.
item.content:encoded:
About 4,200 spill damage claims have been filed over the Inner Harbor oil spill, and part of the fishing grounds closed since September have reopened after testing, officials said Friday.

The count. It is the first public figure for the spill's commercial reach. The claims center run for the owners of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay has taken cleanup and property claims since late September and lost-income claims since mid-November.

The water. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays were closed four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall. Part of those grounds are now open. The rest stay closed pending results.

"The agencies reopened what the testing supports, and nothing more," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Check the current closure maps before you leave the dock. If you have a claim, keep your records in order."

The 90-day mark. Under federal oil spill law, a claim that is denied or not settled within 90 days can be taken to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center. For the earliest lost-income claims, that date arrives next month.

The terminal. "Rendal Terminals continues to cooperate fully," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. He declined to comment on claims or on the investigation.

The cause. On Jan. 4, U.S. officials attributed the intrusion into the tankers' cargo systems to a foreign government they did not name. The Coast Guard has not released its own investigative findings, and officials have not said how the attribution affects liability for the spill.

That question matters to more than the claimants. Owners, charterers, the terminal and their insurers will each read the eventual findings for who bears the cost when a release follows unauthorized access to a ship's systems.

Port condition. Open. The spill response moved to monitoring in late October and no navigation restrictions remain.

Operator notes. Vessels are reminded that reopened fishing grounds mean more small craft working near the channel margins at dawn and dusk.

item.title: Attribution covers tanker intrusion and channel devices; Coast Guard says channel open
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Officials named neither the foreign government nor its methods. The Coast Guard points operators back to last week's advisory on vendor remote access.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. officials on Tuesday attributed the intrusion into the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, to a foreign government they did not name. Officials called the incidents attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael.

Scope. The attribution covers two incidents. The first is the intrusion affecting the two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth, from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released as the storm arrived in September. The second is the devices off the entrance channel: one detonated beside the tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties Oct. 28, and Navy teams rendered a second safe Nov. 5.

Investigation history. The cyber thread dates to Sept. 20, when the Coast Guard first said it was looking into possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems with help from federal cyber teams. On Oct. 30, the Navy said the blast was caused by an explosive device; Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams searched the channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating.

Port condition. Open. The channel returned to service Nov. 11 after a full sweep ended its 14-day closure.

"The channel is open. Today's announcement does not change port conditions," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The Coast Guard will not comment on the details of the attribution."

Operator guidance. The Dec. 28 joint maritime cyber advisory from the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency tells vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. Ruiz said operators should treat it as current. "If you have not completed that review, complete it," she said.

Not released. Officials did not identify the government, describe the evidence or say how the intrusion was carried out. Gulfwater does not speculate on attribution beyond what officials state.

item.title: Corpus Christi 2028: six items on the operator's watch list
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The channel is open and the anchorage is routine. What carries over from 2027 is a set of unfinished reviews, and the next hurricane season is five months out.
item.content:encoded:
Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, New Year's Day: open to all traffic. Waits at the offshore anchorage are routine. For operators planning the year, six items carry over.

1. Vendor access reviews. The Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued a joint maritime cyber advisory Dec. 28 urging vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. "An advisory is only useful if somebody opens the access list and reads it," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Start with who can connect, and remove what you cannot explain."

2. The tanker investigation. The Coast Guard has not released findings on possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. Expect recommendations whenever it reports.

3. The entrance. The FBI investigation into the explosive devices at the Port Aransas entrance is open. No standing restrictions have been announced since the channel reopened in November.

4. Vessel identity. October's AIS anomaly off Port Aransas has no public explanation. "If you see a ship in two places, write it down and send it in," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "Patterns come from many small reports."

5. Drone detection. The port and utility's detection network, announced in October, was expected within 90 days. The Navy's security review at its Texas air stations, ordered in December, is running alongside.

6. Spill claims. The owners' claims center has taken lost-income claims since November. Claims unpaid after 90 days can go to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center, so the first of those dates falls in the coming weeks.

And one that never leaves the list: hurricane season opens in five months. The 2027 lessons are specific. Build timelines from X-Ray. Decide early about ships that stay alongside. Do not treat one entrance channel as a fixed point.

Gulfwater will track each item through the year.

item.title: Coast Guard, CISA advisory: review vendor remote access to cargo systems
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The joint maritime cyber advisory urges vessel operators to check how outside vendors reach cargo systems. It comes three months after the Coast Guard began examining possible remote access to two tankers in Corpus Christi.
item.content:encoded:
The Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued a joint maritime cyber advisory Tuesday urging vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems.

Background. On Sept. 20, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor. An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the two vessels as Hurricane Rafael arrived. On Sept. 22, vendor Brightwake Marine Systems, which maintains tanker cargo systems, reported that its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and said it had revoked all remote access.

"Remote maintenance is a door into the ship. Every operator should know who holds a key, when it's used and how fast it can be taken back," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Review vendor access. Separate cargo control from everything else. Patch what you can. Then review the access again."

"The Coast Guard urges every vessel operator to read this advisory and review vendor remote access to cargo systems," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We will not discuss the details of any open investigation."

Operator notes. In practice, a review of vendor remote access generally starts with an inventory: which vendors hold credentials to cargo-control networks, which of those accounts are still active, and who approves a session before it opens. Operators then look at whether sessions are logged and whether credentials are revoked when a job ends.

Status. The Corpus Christi investigation remains open. Officials have not released any finding on the source of the tanker access. The ship channel is open.

item.title: Rafael by port condition: the three-day sequence that closed Corpus Christi, and the ships that went to sea
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: A year-end reference for operators updating heavy-weather plans: the Coast Guard set X-Ray on Saturday, Sept. 11, closed the port to inbound traffic Sunday and to all traffic Monday. Ships at the anchorage put to sea and came back after landfall.
item.content:encoded:
Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Sunday: open to all traffic. With one hurricane season over and the next about five months out, Gulfwater sets down the sequence that closed the port ahead of Hurricane Rafael, for operators updating heavy-weather plans for 2028.

Saturday, Sept. 11: Port Condition X-Ray, meaning gale-force winds possible within 48 hours. The port stayed open. Ocean-going ships had to plan to leave or obtain approval to stay, and terminals began winding down crude loading.

Sunday, Sept. 12: Port Condition Yankee. The Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic. Ocean-going ships headed out, 14 inbound vessels held at the offshore anchorage, and crude exports halted.

Monday, Sept. 13: Port Condition Zulu. The ship channel closed to all traffic. Ships at the offshore anchorage put to sea to ride out the storm. Two laden tankers stayed at their Inner Harbor berth, with Coast Guard approval.

Tuesday, Sept. 14: Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. as a Category 3 hurricane. Oil was reported spilling at the Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived; Unified Command later estimated about 9,000 barrels released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay.

Friday, Sept. 17: Ships that rode out the storm at sea returned to the offshore anchorage to wait. The channel stayed closed while it was surveyed and the spill was contained.

Thursday, Oct. 14: Partial reopening. Spill decontamination kept the inner channel restricted, and the anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo.

"Port conditions follow the forecast, not the calendar," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "X-Ray is the time to plan. Yankee is the time to move. By Zulu, the channel is shut, and anything still at anchor should be heading for sea room."

Operator notes. Build departure timelines from X-Ray, not Yankee. Confirm sea room and anchorage plans before inbound traffic stops. Expect the restart to depend on channel surveys and, as in 2027, on any spill response inside the port.

Not covered here: the separate closure after the Oct. 28 blast near the Port Aransas jetties, which ended when the channel reopened Nov. 11 after a full sweep.

item.title: Corpus Christi year-end: three maritime security files still open
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Possible remote access to two tankers' cargo systems, an AIS identity anomaly and the jetty blast remain under investigation as the port heads into 2028.
item.content:encoded:
The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been open since Nov. 11, when it reopened after a 14-day closure and a full sweep. Three maritime security files from the fall remain without a public conclusion.

1. Cargo-system access. On Sept. 20, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Federal cyber teams are assisting. On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains tanker cargo systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, revoked all remote access and said it was cooperating. No finding on the source of the access has been released.

2. AIS identity. One night in mid-October, public AIS data placed the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge off Port Aransas, even as the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts later noted the spoofed identity appeared near the entrance channel two weeks before the blast. Officials have declined to comment on any link.

"A vessel identity in two places at once is consistent with spoofing. That's what the data says, and I'm not going to stretch it," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "Who was transmitting is still an open question. Public data alone won't answer it."

3. The jetty blast. An explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28 injured two crew members and closed the channel. The Navy said an explosive device caused it. Navy teams found and rendered safe a second device near the entrance channel Nov. 5. The FBI is investigating.

The Navy on Sunday ordered its Texas air stations to undergo a security review, pointing to the drone reports and the channel attack. The Navy has not discussed the review's scope.

None of the three files has a public conclusion. Gulfwater will report findings as agencies release them.

item.title: Navy orders security review at Texas air stations, citing drone reports and the channel attack
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The review covers Navy installations, not the port. The Coast Guard says port condition is unchanged, and the Navy is not discussing scope.
item.content:encoded:
The Navy on Sunday ordered a security review at its air stations in Texas, citing the drone reports that followed Hurricane Rafael and the attack in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel.

"The Navy has directed a security review at its Texas air stations," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "The review takes account of the reports of drone activity and of the attack in the ship channel. I will not discuss its scope or its timeline."

What it covers. Navy installations. In this area that means Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville.

What it does not cover. The commercial port. The ship channel and its terminals fall under the Coast Guard Captain of the Port, the port authority and the terminal operators.

"The Navy's review does not change port conditions at Corpus Christi," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The channel is open."

Why maritime readers should note it anyway. The review is the first time a federal agency has publicly placed the drone reports and the channel devices in the same sentence. The Navy did not say the two are connected, and neither does Gulfwater. But an installation that sits on the same bay as the channel is now looking at both.

Related. The port and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority announced a drone-detection network for the port and utility corridor in October, expected to be working within 90 days of that announcement.

Open files. The FBI is investigating the explosive devices found at the entrance channel. The Coast Guard investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to two tankers' cargo-control systems remains open. Neither has produced public findings.

Operator notes. No action is required of vessel operators as a result of the Navy's order. Terminals adjoining Navy property should expect to hear from their neighbors. Continue to report unauthorized drone flights and anything unusual on the water to the Coast Guard.

item.title: Editor's notebook: your questions about the entrance channel, answered from the record
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Is the channel safe? What was found? Is the vessel-identity anomaly connected? What is known, what is not, and what Gulfwater will not guess at.
item.content:encoded:
Readers have sent more questions about the Port Aransas entrance than about any subject this year. These are the most common, answered only from what agencies have said on the record.

Is the channel open? Yes. It reopened Nov. 11 after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy and Coast Guard teams. Port condition has been normal since.

What caused the explosion? The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay on Oct. 28. Two crew members were injured.

Was anything else found? Yes. Navy teams found a second device near the entrance channel on Nov. 5 and rendered it safe.

Who put them there? Not known publicly. The FBI is investigating. No agency has named a person, group or motive, and Gulfwater does not speculate on attribution.

What were the devices? The Navy has declined to describe them. We have not asked sources to, and would not publish it.

Is the vessel-identity anomaly connected? In mid-October, public AIS data showed the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts later noted the signal appeared near the entrance channel two weeks before the blast. Officials have declined to comment on any link.

"The timing is a fact. A link is a claim," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "I have the first and not the second. Public data cannot tell you who was transmitting."

Has anything changed for ships? No new standing restrictions have been announced for the entrance. Operators report closer lookout at the jetties, which costs nothing.

What should crews report? Anything unusual on or near the water at the entrance: unlit small craft, objects that do not drift like debris, divers where none are expected. Report to the Coast Guard with time and position.

What we do not know. The source of the devices, whether more will be said about them, and when the FBI will report.

item.title: Inner Harbor spill: shoreline in monitoring, remote-access probe still open
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Nearly three months after about 9,000 barrels of crude escaped two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth, investigators have not released findings on how the cargo systems were accessed.
item.content:encoded:
Status of the Inner Harbor spill response and investigation as of Dec. 10:

Release: About 9,000 barrels of crude from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived in mid-September, according to the Unified Command of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office. Surge and wind carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays; sheen covered about 33 square miles.

Response: Shoreline cleanup moved to a monitoring phase Oct. 28, when inner-channel restrictions for vessel decontamination were lifted. Nueces and Corpus Christi bays are still closed to fishing and shellfish harvesting. The claims center run for the tankers' owners, open since Sept. 26 for cleanup and property damage claims, began taking lost-income claims Nov. 16.

Investigation: The Coast Guard disclosed Sept. 20 that investigators, assisted by federal cyber teams, were looking at possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains tanker cargo-control systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access. No findings have been released.

"The investigation remains open, and we are not in a position to discuss it," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.

Brightwake chief executive Owen Pryce said the company has not switched remote access back on. "We're rebuilding how remote access works here from the ground up, and nothing gets turned back on until we're certain," he said. "We owe that to the crews and to everyone who lives on that water."

Rendal Terminals said it continues to cooperate. "We are cooperating fully with the Unified Command and with investigators," said Victor Lang, a company spokesperson.

Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has supported the investigation, offered general guidance for operators. "Any operator that lets a vendor connect remotely should know who is connecting, when and why, and should be able to shut that door fast," she said.

Gulfwater will report findings when they are released.

item.title: Explainer: how a Coast Guard casualty investigation runs, and when the public sees it
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Readers ask every week when the tanker probe will report. There is no clock on it, and the reasons are built into how these investigations work.
item.content:encoded:
Eleven weeks after about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth, the question Gulfwater hears most is when investigators will say how it happened. This explainer sets out how such an investigation runs.

Who investigates. The Coast Guard investigates marine casualties, including significant oil discharges from vessels. Here it has said federal cyber teams are assisting, because investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems.

What investigators collect. Statements from crew, terminal staff and vendors. Cargo and alarm records from the ships. Logs from shore systems. Physical evidence from valves and control equipment. Where computers are involved, copies of the systems themselves, which take time to examine.

Why it is slow. Evidence comes from several companies in several places, each with lawyers. Technical findings are checked before they are written down. And where a criminal question may exist, some material is held back so as not to prejudice it.

What has been said so far. On Sept. 20 the Coast Guard disclosed the remote-access line of inquiry. On Sept. 22 the vendor Brightwake Marine Systems said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access. Nothing further has been released.

"It will take the time it takes," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Findings are released when the investigation is complete. We do not release them in installments, and we will not characterize an open investigation."

What the public eventually sees. A report of investigation, with findings of fact, conclusions and recommendations. Recommendations can lead to safety alerts or advisories for the whole industry before or after the report itself.

What operators should not do. Wait for the report before acting. The line of inquiry is public. Any operator whose cargo systems can be reached from shore already has enough information to review who holds that access.

Gulfwater will report findings when they are released and will not speculate before then.

item.title: Season-end log: Corpus Christi channel lost weeks to Rafael, spill restrictions and the jetty blast
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The ship channel closed Sept. 13, partly reopened Oct. 14 and closed again for 14 days after the Oct. 28 explosion at the entrance. It has been open since Nov. 11.
item.content:encoded:
The Atlantic hurricane season ends today with the Corpus Christi Ship Channel open, after a fall in which the port lost weeks of normal operations to Hurricane Rafael, an Inner Harbor oil spill and an explosion at the entrance channel.

Sept. 11: Coast Guard sets Port Condition X-Ray ahead of Rafael. The port stays open; terminals wind down crude loading.

Sept. 12: Port Condition Yankee closes the port to inbound traffic. Fourteen vessels hold at the offshore anchorage. Crude exports halt.

Sept. 13: Port Condition Zulu closes the channel to all traffic; anchorage ships put to sea. Two laden tankers remain moored at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval.

Sept. 14 to 15: Rafael makes landfall near Port Aransas. Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth.

Sept. 17: Ships return from sea to the anchorage. The channel stays closed for surveys.

Oct. 14: Channel partly reopens. Inner channel stays restricted for spill decontamination. Anchorage backlog delays relief cargo; MV Gulf Provider berths Oct. 17 with 40 relief containers, about a month late.

Oct. 28: Around 1 a.m., an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties damages the tug and injures two crew. Coast Guard closes the channel. Separately, spill-related inner channel restrictions are lifted as cleanup moves to monitoring.

Oct. 30: Navy says an explosive device caused the blast; a joint Navy-Coast Guard search of the channel is under way.

Nov. 5: Navy teams find a second device near the entrance channel and render it safe.

Nov. 11: Channel reopens after a 14-day closure and full sweep. Exports resume. The next day, a Fort Hood aviation brigade's equipment begins loading onto a sealift ship.

"The channel is open, and we intend to keep it that way," said Javier Salinas, spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The people who work this port had a hard fall. They've earned a quiet winter."

Open items: Investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers' cargo-control systems; the maintenance vendor Brightwake Marine Systems has said its remote credentials were misused. The FBI is investigating the blast.

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, said the service does not comment on open investigations. "Our focus is safe navigation, and the channel is open," she said.

item.title: After two closures in one fall, a relief forwarder rewrites his hurricane playbook
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Terry Akins's containers sat offshore for a month in September and October, and his customers' cargo was held again in November. His new plan starts from a different assumption.
item.content:encoded:
Terry Akins keeps a binder he calls the playbook. This week he is taking pages out of it.

Akins is regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, the freight forwarder whose 40 relief containers on MV Gulf Provider waited at the offshore anchorage through Hurricane Rafael and its aftermath and came ashore Oct. 17, about a month late. In November his customers' cargo was held again when the channel closed for 14 days after the blast at the jetties.

"The old plan said: book the ship, book the berth, wait for the storm to pass," Akins said. "It assumed the channel would open in a few days. Twice this fall that was wrong, for two completely different reasons."

The new plan. Akins described three changes. Split the cargo, so that part moves by sea and part is staged inland within a day's trucking. Name a second port in the standby contract, with the right to divert before the ship joins a queue. And decide the diversion point in advance. "Once you are in the line at the anchorage, you have already lost the choice," he said.

The cost. More warehousing, more trucking and a contract that is harder to negotiate. Akins said the agencies he works for have not objected. "They remember where the boxes were on Oct. 4," he said. "They were looking at the beach."

The port's view. "We understand why customers plan alternatives, and we would in their place," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Our job is to be reliable enough that the alternative stays in the binder."

Port condition. Open. The backlog from the November closure has worked down and waits at the anchorage are back to what operators call routine.

For other operators. The lesson is not specific to relief cargo. Any plan that treats a single entrance channel as a fixed point should say what happens when it is not.

Akins said the binder will be thinner. "Fewer pages. More phone numbers," he said.

item.title: Two months on, Brightwake's remote access to tanker cargo systems remains switched off
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The vendor revoked all remote connections in September after its credentials were misused. Its chief executive says technicians now attend ships in person and nothing reconnects until the rebuild is finished.
item.content:encoded:
Brightwake Marine Systems has not restored remote access to any customer vessel, two months after it said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, chief executive Owen Pryce told Gulfwater.

Background. Brightwake maintains tanker cargo-control systems. On Sept. 20 the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the tankers from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Two days later Brightwake said its credentials had been misused, revoked all remote access and said it was cooperating.

Status. Unchanged, Pryce said. "Every remote connection we had is off. Our technicians go to the ship. That is slower and more expensive, and slower and more expensive is acceptable," he said.

Pryce said the company is rebuilding how it connects to vessels before turning anything back on. He would not give a date. "I am not going to promise a month and then miss it. When it comes back, each session will have a named person on our side and a named person on the ship who agreed to it," he said.

He said the company still does not know who misused the credentials. "That is a question for the investigators. We have given them everything we have," he said.

The federal view. Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is supporting the investigation, would not discuss the case. Her general advice to operators has not changed. "Know who can connect to your vessel, when they connect and why," she said. "And be able to cut that connection in minutes, not days."

Investigation. Open. No finding on the source of the access has been released.

Operator notes. Ask every vendor with shipboard access for a list of accounts and the date each was last used. Remove what is not needed. Require the master's or chief officer's consent before any remote session opens on a cargo system.

item.title: Back on the tow wire: Corrin Bay's master returns to the channel on a borrowed boat
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Capt. Ray Dupree went back to work this week, three weeks after the blast at the jetties. He says the job is the same. The way he looks at the water is not.
item.content:encoded:
Capt. Ray Dupree went back to work this week on a boat that is not his.

Dupree, 56, is master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, operated by Laguna Towing. Corrin Bay has been out of service since an explosion off its port bow near the Port Aransas jetties in the early hours of Oct. 28. The Navy said an explosive device caused it. The channel stayed closed for two weeks and reopened Nov. 11 after a full sweep.

The company has put Dupree on another of its tugs. He has run tugs in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years, and he said the first assist felt like any other. "Line up, make fast, listen to the pilot, push when he says push," he said. "The work is the same. I look at the water differently."

He described the difference without drama. He slows his eyes down at the jetties. He asks the deck crew to call out anything floating, whatever it looks like. "We always watched for logs and pots. Now I want to hear about a plastic bag," he said.

Two of his crew were hurt that night. Deckhand Eddie Fontenot, 29, is recovering with his arm still in a cast. "He is mending and bored, which is the right order," Dupree said.

The channel he came back to is busy. Tankers held inside during the closure have sailed, the line at the offshore anchorage is working down, and military sealift moved through last week.

Dupree said harbor crews talk about the blast less than outsiders expect. "Tug men talk about the weather and the pilots and whose turn it is to cook," he said. "It is there, though. You see it when a boat comes in past the jetties and everybody on deck goes quiet for a minute."

He would not discuss the investigation. He said he expects Corrin Bay to work again.

"She took it and stayed up," he said. "I would like to be standing in her wheelhouse when she goes back out."

item.title: Spill claims center begins taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The center run for the tankers' owners has handled cleanup and property claims since September. Claims left unpaid after 90 days can go to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.
item.content:encoded:
The claims center run for the owners of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay began taking lost-income claims Tuesday from commercial fishers and shoreline businesses affected by the Inner Harbor oil spill.

What changed. The center opened in September for cleanup costs and property damage, as federal oil spill law requires. It now also takes claims for income lost because of the spill.

Who may claim. People and businesses whose earnings fell because of the oil. In practice that means bay shrimpers, oystermen, guides, bait and tackle shops, marinas and waterfront businesses. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed by state agencies since four days after landfall.

The 90-day rule. A claim goes first to the party responsible for the spill. If it is denied, or is not settled within 90 days, the claimant can take it to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

"If the spill cost you income, file," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Bring what you have: trip tickets, logbooks, tax returns, fuel receipts. The better the records, the faster it moves. The closures themselves are set by the state health and wildlife agencies, and they stay until testing says otherwise."

The spill. The Unified Command estimated about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived.

"Rendal Terminals continues to cooperate fully with the Unified Command and investigators," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. He referred questions about claims to the claims center.

For vessel operators. Ships that were delayed by the storm closure or by the inner-channel restrictions should take advice on whether their losses fall under the same law or under their charter parties. Those are different questions with different answers.

Not resolved. The Coast Guard's investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems remains open. Its outcome may bear on who ultimately pays.

item.title: Week in review: Corpus Christi channel reopens, sealift sails, backlog works down
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: A summary of port conditions after the 14-day closure, for operators planning the week ahead.
item.content:encoded:
Port condition, Corpus Christi, Sunday: channel open to all traffic; movements sequenced by the Captain of the Port and pilots; crude loadings under way; no Coast Guard restrictions announced beyond normal operations.

Reopening. The Coast Guard reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel on Thursday, Nov. 11, after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams working with the Coast Guard. The closure began after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties Oct. 28. Navy teams rendered a second device safe near the entrance Nov. 5.

Backlog. Vessels that held offshore during the closure began moving in Thursday under a sequenced plan. Public AIS shows the queue shrinking steadily; no official count has been released. The pattern resembles the October restart after Hurricane Rafael, when an anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo. One difference: inner-channel spill restrictions, which slowed that earlier restart, were lifted in late October.

Sealift. A sealift ship began loading a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment Friday. The Army said the equipment would sail over the next five days for an overseas rotation. The Army has released no ship details, and Gulfwater will not report them.

Exports. Crude loadings resumed Thursday. Market analysts expect a catch-up period as onshore storage drains and rebooked cargoes return. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

Open questions. The FBI is investigating the Oct. 28 blast. Officials continue to decline comment on any link between the explosion and the mid-October AIS anomaly, in which the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge was broadcast near the entrance channel while the vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Gulfwater makes no assessment of a connection.

Outlook. Absent new notices, operators should plan for normal port conditions with residual sequencing delays early in the week. Gulfwater will report changes as the Coast Guard issues them.

item.title: 60-day assessment: Corpus Christi Bay back below state hydrocarbon standard; emergency phase of spill response closed
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: State and federal regulators put bay readings at 0.03 milligrams per liter and say most Nueces Bay shoreline cleanup is done. Fishing closures stay until testing supports reopening.
item.content:encoded:
Two months after crude from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, state and federal regulators on Saturday closed the emergency phase of the Inner Harbor oil spill response.

Water. The 60-day remediation assessment by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and EPA Region 6 puts total petroleum hydrocarbons in Corpus Christi Bay at 0.03 milligrams per liter, below the state surface water standard of 0.05.

Shoreline. Cleanup of the Nueces Bay shoreline is nearly complete. Minor tar ball accumulation persists on about 0.4 kilometers of shoreline near the Nueces Bay Causeway and will be handled in the 2028 spring shoreline maintenance program, the assessment said.

Drinking water. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant has stayed within all regulatory limits for 52 consecutive days.

Long term. Monitoring of Nueces Bay seagrass beds and oyster reefs continues under a separate natural resource damage agreement with the tankers' owners. Cleanup, wildlife rehabilitation and fishing-loss figures in the assessment go to those proceedings.

Closures. Fishing and shellfish harvesting closures remain in effect until state testing supports reopening.

"Closing the emergency phase is a milestone, and it is a real one," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "The water column is where it should be. The closures are a separate decision, and they follow the test results."

Background. The Unified Command estimated the release at about 9,000 barrels from the two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Cleanup moved to monitoring on Oct. 28. The Coast Guard has been examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems since September; no findings have been released.

Operator notes. The assessment does not change port status. The ship channel reopened Thursday after the closure that followed the explosion near the Port Aransas jetties.

item.title: First full day after reopening: crude, cargo and military sealift share the Corpus Christi channel
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Traffic resumed under Coast Guard and pilot direction. Questions about the mid-October AIS anomaly near the entrance remain unanswered.
item.content:encoded:
Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: channel open to all traffic under Coast Guard order issued Thursday; movements sequenced by the Captain of the Port and pilots; crude loadings resumed.

The first full day after a 14-day closure saw inbound tankers that had held offshore enter through the Port Aransas jetties alongside general cargo. A sealift ship began loading a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment, which the Army said will sail over the next five days for an overseas rotation.

"Traffic is moving safely and in order," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are asking every operator for patience while the backlog clears. The order of movements is set for safety, not for any one customer."

The reopening followed a full sweep by Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams working with the Coast Guard. The search began after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties Oct. 28, and teams found and rendered safe a second device near the entrance Nov. 5.

Public AIS displays on Friday showed a dense but orderly pattern at the entrance, with vessels transmitting normally. That contrasts with the night of Oct. 14-15, when the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge was broadcast near the entrance channel while the vessel itself reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts call that pattern consistent with spoofing.

"The traffic today looks like a port getting back to work," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst. "That doesn't answer anything about mid-October. Those questions are still open, and public data alone isn't going to close them."

Officials have declined to comment on any link between the AIS observations and the blast. The FBI is investigating the explosion. Gulfwater makes no assessment of a connection.

Operators should continue to monitor Coast Guard notices for the movement schedule as the backlog clears.

item.title: Corpus Christi Ship Channel reopens after 14-day closure and full sweep
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The Coast Guard lifts the closure order Thursday morning. Exports resume, and the first movements are sequenced with the pilots.
item.content:encoded:
Port condition, Corpus Christi, Thursday morning: OPEN. The Coast Guard Captain of the Port has lifted the order that closed the ship channel on Oct. 28.

The 14-day closure ended after Navy and Coast Guard teams completed a full sweep of the channel. Crude exports are resuming.

"The Captain of the Port has lifted the closure order," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The first movements are being sequenced with the pilots. Mariners should read the notice in full and follow the directions of the vessel traffic service."

The Navy. "The sweep of the channel is complete and the channel is clear," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. She declined to add to earlier statements about what the teams found.

Background. An explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties closed the channel. The Navy said an explosive device caused it. Teams found a second device near the entrance channel on Nov. 5 and rendered it safe. The FBI is investigating.

The port. "Berths are clear and terminals are staffed," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The plan for the first days was written while we waited. Today we work the plan."

What is different from October. When the channel partly reopened after Hurricane Rafael, spill decontamination kept the inner channel restricted and the backlog took days to move. Those restrictions were lifted Oct. 28. This restart has one constraint, the entrance, and it is now open.

Who moves. Loaded tankers held inside since the closure. Ships waiting at the offshore anchorage. Military sealift for the Fort Hood aviation brigade, whose port movement has been delayed twice.

Operator notes. Expect one-way sequencing and a slow first day. Confirm readiness with agents before requesting a pilot. Keep a sharp lookout at the entrance and report anything unusual to the Coast Guard.

Gulfwater will publish a first-day traffic report Friday.

item.title: Corpus Christi entrance stays closed into second week; no change in port condition
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Inbound traffic continues to hold offshore while Navy teams sweep the entrance channel at Port Aransas. Inner-channel spill restrictions were lifted before the closure, so the entrance is the only constraint.
item.content:encoded:
Port condition, Corpus Christi, as of Tuesday morning: entrance channel closed under Coast Guard order; deep-draft movements suspended in both directions; crude loadings halted. No reopening date issued.

The closure entered its 13th day Tuesday. It began after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been searching the channel with the Coast Guard since, and rendered a second device safe near the entrance Friday.

"There is no change in port condition today," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The Captain of the Port will reopen the channel when the search is complete. Mariners will receive notice before any change, and we ask operators not to plan on rumor."

One complication from earlier this fall is gone. Restrictions on the inner channel, imposed while vessels were decontaminated after the September oil spill, were lifted Oct. 28 as cleanup moved to monitoring. When the entrance reopens, operators will not face a second set of spill restrictions inside the harbor.

The backlog will matter. When the channel partly reopened Oct. 14 after Hurricane Rafael, an anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo, including MV Gulf Provider, for several days. The same sequencing problem is building now, with vessels of every kind holding for the same entrance.

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the port is working with the Coast Guard and pilots on a restart plan. "We are not going to say when, because that isn't our call," Salinas said. "We can say we will be ready. Berths are clear, terminals are staffed, and the plan for the first days is written."

Gulfwater will report changes in port condition as they are issued.

item.title: Explainer: what a Captain of the Port closure order does, and who it binds
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The entrance at Port Aransas has been shut for 11 days. The order behind the closure applies to every vessel, and it ends only when the Coast Guard says so in writing.
item.content:encoded:
Port condition, Corpus Christi, Sunday: entrance channel closed, day 11. No reopening date issued. Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel Friday and rendered it safe; the search continues.

Readers have asked what, in law, is keeping ships out. The short answer is an order from the Coast Guard Captain of the Port.

The authority. Federal law gives the Captain of the Port power to control vessel movement to protect a waterway, including by closing it or by setting a safety or security zone around a hazard. The order needs no vote and no hearing. It takes effect when issued.

Who it binds. Everyone. Tankers, tows, fishing boats, ferries and recreational craft. A zone around the jetties is as closed to a skiff as to a crude carrier.

"The order applies to every vessel, commercial or recreational," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "It ends by written notice from the Captain of the Port. We ask operators to wait for the notice and not to plan on what they hear on the radio or the dock."

How it ends. In this case, when the search of the channel is complete. The Navy is running that search with the Coast Guard.

"Our teams will continue until the search is complete," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "I am not going to describe methods or what was recovered. The standard is that the channel is safe for the ships that use it."

What a reopening notice usually contains. The time the order lifts. Any conditions on the first transits, such as daylight only or one-way traffic. Any zone that remains in force. Operators should read it for what it keeps as well as what it lifts.

Operator notes. Entering a closed zone can bring civil and criminal penalties. Agents should confirm they are on the Coast Guard's notice distribution. Crude exports remain halted until the entrance reopens.

item.title: Second device rendered safe near the Port Aransas jetties; Coast Guard keeps channel closed
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Navy teams recovered a second explosive device Friday. Port condition unchanged: entrance closed to all traffic, no reopening date.
item.content:encoded:
Navy teams located a second explosive device near the entrance channel at Port Aransas Friday and rendered it safe, the Navy and Coast Guard said. No injuries were reported. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed to all traffic.

Port condition as of Friday afternoon: the entrance is closed under Coast Guard order. Inbound and outbound deep-draft movements are suspended. Crude loadings at the port are halted. No reopening date has been issued.

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, said the Captain of the Port would not lift the closure until the full search is complete. "A second find does not shorten the process. It confirms why we follow it," Ruiz said. "When the channel opens, mariners will receive notice through the usual channels."

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, said Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams continue to work with the Coast Guard. She declined to describe the device or its position, citing safety and the investigation.

The first device detonated around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 alongside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties, injuring two of its crew and damaging the tug. The FBI is investigating that blast.

As Gulfwater reported Monday, public AIS data shows the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcast near the entrance channel overnight Oct. 14-15, while the vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts describe that pattern as consistent with spoofing. Asked Friday whether investigators were examining the AIS observations, Ruiz said the Coast Guard would not comment on any link. Gulfwater makes no assessment of a connection.

Operators with vessels holding offshore should continue to monitor Coast Guard broadcast notices for changes in port condition. After a long closure, a staged restart is typical, with the order of vessel movements set by the Coast Guard and the port.

item.title: 'Count heads first': Corrin Bay's master and deckhand on the night at the jetties
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Capt. Ray Dupree has not been back on the water. Deckhand Eddie Fontenot is recovering from a broken arm and a concussion. Both describe a routine job until it wasn't.
item.content:encoded:
Capt. Ray Dupree has run tugs in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. Since the early hours of Oct. 28 he has not run one at all.

Dupree, 56, is master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, operated by Laguna Towing. The tug was working near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. when an explosion went off off its port bow. The Navy has since said an explosive device caused it. The channel has been closed for a week.

"It was a regular job on a regular night," Dupree said. "Then the whole boat jumped. Count heads first. That is what you are taught and that is what I did."

Two of his crew were hurt. One was deckhand Eddie Fontenot, 29, who has a broken arm and a concussion.

Fontenot spoke by phone Tuesday. He kept his answers short. "I remember the noise. Then I was on the deck and my arm was wrong," he said. "Cap was there quick. Everybody was there quick. I'm grateful for that."

He said he does not remember much of the ride in.

Dupree has been visiting him most days. With Corrin Bay out of service, the captain has time. He said he does not like it. "A tug man with nothing to push is not good company," he said.

On the Navy's finding, Dupree chose his words. "Somebody put that there. I have been turning that over for a week," he said. "I am not going to say more than that, because I don't know more than that. The Navy and the FBI are working it. I will tell them anything they ask."

He said harbor crews have always watched the water at the jetties for logs, crab pots and small boats without lights. "You look for what can foul a wheel or hole a hull. Nobody trained us to look for this," he said.

Fontenot said he wants to go back to work. "I want to go back. Not this week," he said.

item.title: Spoofed vessel identity appeared near the entrance channel at Port Aransas two weeks before jetty blast
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Public AIS data places the borrowed fishing-vessel identity close to the entrance channel in mid-October. The Coast Guard declined to comment on any connection to the Oct. 28 explosion.
item.content:encoded:
Public AIS records reviewed by maritime analysts show that the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge was broadcast near the entrance channel at Port Aransas overnight Oct. 14-15, about two weeks before an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel.

Gulfwater reported the anomaly Oct. 22. On the same night the identity was logged off Port Aransas, the vessel itself reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Independent analyst Ian McCready, a former Coast Guard watchstander, said then that the pattern was consistent with identity spoofing. A closer review of the public track places the signal near the entrance channel.

"The data tells you where a signal was. It does not tell you who sent it or why," McCready said Monday. "Two weeks is a long gap, and I would be careful drawing a straight line. But the location is close to the entrance, and that is worth writing down."

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, declined to comment on any link between the AIS observations and the explosion. "We are not going to discuss matters under investigation," Ruiz said. "Our focus is the safety of the waterway."

The Navy said Saturday that the blast was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams and the Coast Guard are working the channel jointly; the FBI is investigating.

Port status as of Monday morning: the channel remains closed at the entrance, with no reopening date announced. Crude loadings at the port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, have been halted since the closure. Inbound traffic is holding offshore.

AIS is a cooperative system. A transponder broadcasts whatever identity it is programmed with, and shore and satellite receivers record it. Analysts detect spoofing by finding the same identity in two places at once, as in this case. Gulfwater has not identified the vessel that transmitted the Pelican Ridge identity and makes no assessment of who was aboard.

item.title: Navy EOD and mine countermeasures teams join Coast Guard search of Corpus Christi channel
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Navy confirms an explosive device caused Thursday's blast beside tug Corrin Bay. Channel remains closed to all traffic; crude exports halted; no reopening estimate.
item.content:encoded:
Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel with the Coast Guard after the Navy confirmed Saturday that an explosive device caused Thursday's blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties.

Status as of Saturday:

Channel: Closed to all vessel traffic. Search: Navy EOD and mine countermeasures teams with the Coast Guard; no timeline given.

Exports: Crude exports halted again. Investigation: FBI investigating. Reopening: No estimate.

"Our teams will search methodically," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "That takes the time it takes. We will not discuss the device."

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said mariners should follow broadcast notices. "Vessels at the anchorage should remain clear of the entrance channel and monitor notices for changes," she said.

The Unified Command lifted inner-channel spill decontamination restrictions Thursday, the same day as the blast, but the closure has kept all traffic stopped. The channel had partly reopened Oct. 14 after closing for Hurricane Rafael. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement, postponed by the hurricane, has been delayed again.

Background: The port closed to inbound traffic two days before Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall, with 14 vessels holding offshore; the channel closed to all traffic the next day. The partial reopening on Oct. 14 restored traffic after a month, and the relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider berthed Oct. 17 after weeks in the anchorage backlog. The port accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports.

Two crew members were hurt and the tug damaged. Officials have not said who placed the device or how long it had been in the channel. Gulfwater will report search results and channel status as they are released.

item.title: Day two of the entrance closure: tug master describes blast off the port bow; cause still unknown
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The harbor tug Corrin Bay is out of service and two of its crew are hurt. The Coast Guard has given no cause and no reopening time, and ships are holding on both sides of the jetties.
item.content:encoded:
Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: ship channel closed to all traffic by Captain of the Port order. No reopening time issued.

What happened. An explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Thursday. The tug was damaged and two crew members were injured. The cause is unknown.

The master. "It came off the port bow," said Capt. Ray Dupree, 56, master of Corrin Bay, which is operated by Laguna Towing. Dupree has run tugs in the ship channel for 30 years. "First thing you do is count heads. I counted, and two of mine were hurt. Then you find out if the boat is going to stay under you. She did."

Dupree declined to guess at a cause. "I know what I felt. I don't know what it was," he said. "I'll let the people whose job that is tell me."

The Coast Guard. "The channel is closed by order of the Captain of the Port," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The cause of the explosion is not known. We will not set a reopening time until we understand what happened and are satisfied the waterway is safe."

Timing. The closure came the same day spill cleanup moved to monitoring and the last inner-channel restrictions were lifted. On Thursday the port lost its last spill restriction and its only entrance within hours of each other.

Who is waiting. Loaded tankers inside. Inbound ships at the offshore anchorage. Military cargo: the Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement, postponed in September, is delayed again.

Operator notes. All movements through the entrance are suspended, including small craft. Vessels inside should remain at their berths. Vessels offshore should hold at the anchorage and keep clear of the jetties and of Coast Guard units on scene. Report anything unusual seen near the entrance this week, with times, to the Coast Guard.

Gulfwater will report changes in port condition as they are issued.

item.title: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed after explosion beside tug at entrance jetties
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Coast Guard closes the channel to all traffic. Tug Corrin Bay damaged, two crew injured, cause unknown. Unified Command lifts inner-channel spill restrictions the same day.
item.content:encoded:
The Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all vessel traffic early Thursday after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties at about 0100 local time. The tug was damaged and two crew members were injured. The cause is unknown.

Status as of Thursday morning, per Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Unified Command:

Channel: Closed to all vessel traffic until further notice.

Inner channel: Spill decontamination restrictions lifted Thursday as the Unified Command moved cleanup to a monitoring phase. The change has no practical effect while the channel is closed.

Anchorage: Vessels holding offshore east of Port Aransas. Reopening: No estimate.

"The channel will remain closed until the Coast Guard determines it is safe for navigation," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector public affairs officer. "Updates will be issued through broadcast notices to mariners. We will not speculate on the cause."

The closure ends a two-week partial reopening. The channel closed to inbound traffic two days before Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall, with 14 vessels holding offshore, closed to all traffic the next day and partly reopened Oct. 14, with the inner channel restricted for decontamination after an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers moored at the Rendal Terminals berth.

Before the blast, the inner-channel restriction and the anchorage backlog had been the main constraints on traffic since Oct. 14; the backlog held the relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider offshore until Oct. 17.

Gulfwater has not confirmed what the tug was doing at the time of the explosion, and the Coast Guard has not described the extent of the damage.

About half of U.S. crude exports load at this port. An extended closure would hold tankers at inner berths and at the anchorage. Gulfwater will report changes to channel status as notices are issued.

item.title: GPS interference near Corpus Christi: what the FAA notice says, and what it means on a ship's bridge
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Pilots have reported interference within about 40 miles of the city. The notice is for aviators, but the habits that protect a flight deck are the same ones that protect a wheelhouse.
item.content:encoded:
Pilots have reported GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi, and the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a notice to aviators. Relief flights are continuing on backup navigation.

"Pilots operating near Corpus Christi have reported interference with GPS, and we have issued a notice so crews plan for it," said Lynn Carver, a regional spokesperson for the FAA. "Aircraft have other ways to navigate, and flights are continuing."

The notice is addressed to aviation. Gulfwater readers have asked what it means afloat. What follows is general seamanship, not a report of any incident on the water.

Why mariners should care. Satellite positioning feeds more than the chart display. On a modern bridge it also feeds the AIS transponder, the radar overlay and the clocks that other equipment relies on. When the input is wrong, several screens can be wrong together, and they will agree with each other.

What to do. Fix position by more than one method. In the approaches to Corpus Christi that means radar ranges and bearings, visual bearings on the jetties and ranges, and the depth sounder checked against the chart. Compare, and write the comparison down. Treat a sudden jump in position, speed or time as a warning, not a glitch.

"The Coast Guard expects mariners to fix their position by all available means, every watch, whether or not anyone has reported a problem," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. She declined to discuss the interference reports.

Pilotage. Ships transiting the channel carry a pilot who works largely by eye, radar and local knowledge. That is the strongest protection in confined water.

Port condition. Partly open; inner-channel restrictions for spill decontamination remain.

Operator notes. Brief bridge teams before arrival. Report suspected interference to the Coast Guard with time, position and what the equipment showed. Do not adjust equipment settings to make an alarm go away.

item.title: Fishing vessel's identity broadcast off Port Aransas while it reported a position 600 nm away
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Public AIS data show FV Pelican Ridge's identity transmitting off Port Aransas on the night of Oct. 14-15 while the vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. An analyst calls it consistent with identity spoofing.
item.content:encoded:
Public Automatic Identification System data show the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas on the night of Oct. 14-15, while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away, according to an analysis by independent maritime security analyst Ian McCready.

McCready, a former Coast Guard watchstander who reviews public AIS feeds for anomalies, said both tracks cannot belong to one hull. "A vessel can't be in two places 600 nautical miles apart at the same time," he said. "When one identity shows up in both, the pattern is consistent with identity spoofing. Something off Port Aransas was transmitting an identity that wasn't its own."

AIS transponders broadcast a vessel's identity, position, course and speed over VHF radio. Shore stations and satellites collect the messages, and traffic services, port operators and other ships use them to build a picture of who is where. The system reports what the transmitter tells it. "AIS is a self-report," McCready said. "It's very good at telling you what a ship says about itself. On its own, it can't tell you whether that's true."

McCready cautioned against conclusions beyond the data. "I can tell you the tracks are inconsistent and that the inconsistency fits spoofing," he said. "I can't tell you what vessel was transmitting or why. I'd want radar or imagery before I said anything more."

Gulfwater has not independently identified the vessel that was transmitting.

Context: The anchorage off Port Aransas, where tankers routinely wait for berths, has held a queue since ships that put to sea for Hurricane Rafael returned three days after its Sept. 14 landfall; 14 vessels were waiting there when the port closed to inbound traffic two days before the storm. The channel partly reopened Oct. 14, with the inner channel still restricted for spill decontamination.

False identities degrade the traffic picture that mariners and port operators rely on for collision avoidance and vessel management, particularly in a crowded anchorage. Gulfwater will report any official response.

item.title: Port and utility to field drone-detection network across infrastructure corridor
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The joint initiative follows a federal report on unauthorized drone flights before Rafael. The sensing network is expected to be working within 90 days.
item.content:encoded:
The Port of Corpus Christi Authority and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority will deploy a drone-detection network across the port and utility corridor, the two agencies announced Saturday.

What it is. A radio-frequency sensing and direction-finding network at multiple sites, operated in coordination with the Federal Aviation Administration and Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations. The agencies said Sentinel Airspace Inc. was selected as the technology provider after a competitive evaluation.

When. The network is expected to be operational within 90 days.

Why. The announcement cites a recommendation in the joint FAA and CBP report on unauthorized drone activity before Hurricane Rafael. The two federal agencies confirmed in late September that investigators had identified multiple unauthorized flights in the Corpus Christi area in the period before the storm. Gulfwater reported Sept. 30, citing sources familiar with the investigation, that authorities were examining whether drones had flown over the port and at least one power utility facility in the week before landfall.

"We would rather know what is flying over the docks than guess," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "This is a detection system. It tells us and our federal partners what is in the air and where it came from. We are not going to discuss where the sensors sit."

What it is not. The agencies described a network that detects and locates. They did not describe any capability to interfere with aircraft, which is tightly restricted under federal law.

Port condition. Partly open. Inner-channel restrictions for spill decontamination remain, and the anchorage backlog is still working down.

Operator notes. Terminals that fly their own drones for inspections or security should expect to be asked to register those flights once the network is running, so authorized aircraft can be told from unauthorized ones. Ship operators should remind crews that flying personal drones from vessels in port is not permitted without authorization.

The FBI investigation into the pre-storm flights remains open.

item.title: MV Gulf Provider berths and lands 40 relief containers, about a month late
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The cargo was booked before Rafael and waited offshore through the closure and the backlog that followed the partial reopening. Inner-channel restrictions remain.
item.content:encoded:
MV Gulf Provider berthed at Corpus Christi on Sunday and unloaded 40 relief containers, about a month after the cargo was meant to arrive.

The containers were booked before Hurricane Rafael by the freight forwarder Gulf Relief Logistics. The ship waited at the offshore anchorage through the storm closure, then waited again in the backlog that built when the channel partly reopened Thursday.

"Those boxes were booked five days before landfall. They touched the dock today," said Terry Akins, the company's regional manager. "Nobody on that ship did anything wrong. Nobody at the port did anything wrong. We had a plan that depended on one channel, and the channel was shut."

Port condition. Partly open. Spill decontamination continues to restrict the inner channel, which limits how many ships can work the Inner Harbor berths and slows the turn of those that do.

Why relief cargo waited after the reopening. A partial reopening does not clear an anchorage. Transits resumed under conditions, and the line offshore held weeks of arrivals. Sequencing put ships through by draft, berth and readiness as well as priority.

"Getting that ship alongside was a priority for us within the limits we are working under," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The backlog is real and it is shrinking. Every day the channel stays open, the line gets shorter."

What was aboard. Akins described the cargo as general relief supplies consigned to agencies working in the three coastal counties. Trucks began moving containers off the terminal the same afternoon, he said.

Operator notes. Expect the backlog at the anchorage to persist while the inner channel stays restricted. Confirm decontamination requirements with the Coast Guard and the terminal before arrival. Ships bound for berths outside the restricted reach should say so early; it affects their place in the line.

Gulfwater first reported on the forwarder's standby contracts in August.

item.title: Port authority: ships to move by priority as channel partly reopens; no date for the inner channel
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The port's afternoon statement fills in the morning's Coast Guard notice: outer and bay reaches cleared after surveys, the offshore queue to be worked by priority, relief cargo delayed, and six security cameras along the Inner Harbor still offline.
item.content:encoded:
The Port of Corpus Christi Authority on Thursday afternoon confirmed the partial reopening of the ship channel, 30 days after Hurricane Rafael closed it, and set out how the first traffic will be handled.

What is open. The Coast Guard cleared the outer and bay reaches of the channel after surveys of channel depth and aids to navigation, the port said.

What is not. The inner channel remains restricted while vessels and berths affected by the Inner Harbor oil spill are decontaminated. No date has been set for lifting that restriction.

The queue. Ships waiting at the offshore anchorage will be brought in by priority. The port said the backlog will delay some cargo, including relief shipments. Gulfwater reported Thursday morning that the delayed cargo includes the 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider.

Security systems. Six port security cameras along the Inner Harbor remain offline pending replacement parts, the statement said.

Investigation. The Coast Guard investigation into the tanker oil release remains open.

"The outer and bay reaches are open, the inner channel is restricted, and the line offshore gets worked in order of priority," said Javier Salinas, spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "It is a partial reopening. We are not calling it anything else."

Operator notes. For crude shippers the distinction matters. Rendal Terminals and the other Inner Harbor docks sit behind the restricted reach, so Thursday's change first helps vessels bound for berths outside it. Charterers with ships at the anchorage should confirm berth status with their agents before assuming a slot. Vessels that do transit the inner channel remain subject to the Unified Command's decontamination requirements, the Coast Guard said earlier Thursday.

Gulfwater will report the order of the first arrivals as the port releases it.

item.title: Corpus Christi channel partly reopens; inner reaches stay restricted for decontamination
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The Coast Guard eased the storm closure Thursday, 30 days after Hurricane Rafael's landfall. Vessels bound for inner berths face decontamination requirements, and the offshore queue remains.
item.content:encoded:
The Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel on Thursday, 30 days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island. The inner channel remains restricted while vessels are decontaminated following the Inner Harbor oil spill, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said.

"Traffic will move in a controlled sequence," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector public affairs officer. "Vessels transiting the inner channel remain subject to decontamination requirements set by the Unified Command. Mariners should monitor broadcast notices for current conditions before getting under way."

The port shut to inbound traffic two days before landfall, with 14 vessels at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas and crude exports stopped; the channel closed to all traffic a day later. Two laden tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, remained moored at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor with Coast Guard approval.

The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office has estimated that about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the two tankers as the storm arrived. Surge and wind carried the oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, with sheen covering roughly 33 square miles at its extent.

Thursday's change does not clear the anchorage. The port said the backlog is delaying relief cargo, including MV Gulf Provider, which carries 40 relief containers booked before the storm.

Neither the Coast Guard nor the port gave a date for lifting the inner-channel restriction. Ruiz said conditions would be reviewed as decontamination continues and that changes would be announced through broadcast notices to mariners.
