The port accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports, so the rate at which tankers can move between inner berths and open water will be watched closely by shippers and charterers. Gulfwater will update channel status as notices are issued.

item.title: When the channel opens, who moves first? Relief cargo, crude and a long line offshore
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: No date has been set. But the order of the first arrivals is already being argued, and a relief ship with 40 containers has been waiting since before the storm.
item.content:encoded:
Port condition, Corpus Christi, Sunday: closed to all traffic. No reopening date issued.

The line. Ships that rode out Hurricane Rafael at sea have been waiting at the offshore anchorage since the week of landfall. Others have arrived since. When the Coast Guard reopens the channel, they cannot all move at once, and the first transits are likely to carry draft or daylight limits.

One ship in that line is MV Gulf Provider, carrying 40 relief containers booked before the storm by the freight forwarder Gulf Relief Logistics.

"I have forty boxes of relief supplies looking at the beach," said Terry Akins, the company's regional manager. "I understand the channel is closed for good reasons. I also know what is in those boxes and who is waiting for it. When there is a sequence, relief should be in front."

How sequencing works. The Captain of the Port sets the conditions. Within them, pilots, agents and terminals build the order. Time at anchor counts, but so do draft, berth readiness and cargo priority. A deep-laden tanker and a container ship do not need the same water or the same dock.

"We have a restart sequence drafted with the pilots, and it changes as the picture changes," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Relief cargo is on the list near the top. The first day will be slow by design."

What has changed. The Unified Command has said the main slick from the Inner Harbor spill is contained and primary skimming is finished. The fishing closure in the bays has been extended. Containment removes one obstacle to navigation; it does not by itself reopen the channel.

Operator notes. Confirm draft, readiness and berth with agents now, so the ship can be slotted quickly. Expect conditions on transits near the spill site in the Inner Harbor. Expect the backlog to take days to work down after the first ship moves.

item.title: Tanker cargo-systems probe continues with few public details
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: More than two weeks after the Coast Guard said it was examining possible unauthorized remote access, investigators have released no findings. The vendor's remote access remains off.
item.content:encoded:
Status, Oct. 7: Investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay ongoing. No findings released. Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said Sept. 20 that investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers' cargo-control systems, with federal cyber teams assisting. The laden tankers were moored at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor when Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude were released.

On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that supports tanker cargo-control systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, that it had revoked all remote access and that it was cooperating with investigators.

Neither the Coast Guard nor federal cyber officials have released findings since.

"The investigation is active and thorough, and we will not release partial information," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Sector Corpus Christi public affairs officer. "When we can share findings responsibly, we will."

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is still supporting the Coast Guard, said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the agency. She declined to discuss the investigation but offered general advice for any operator of connected industrial systems. "Know what's connected to your systems. Keep it patched. Know who can get in from outside, and turn off what you don't need," Tran said. "None of that is new advice. It's just advice that's easy to put off."

Technical note: Investigations involving shipboard control systems typically require forensic review of system logs, network equipment and vendor records, and can take weeks or months. Findings may be shared with operators and regulators before any public release.

Port conditions: Channel closed to all traffic since Sept. 13. Crude exports halted. The Coast Guard has not announced a reopening date. Spill response continues in the Inner Harbor and the bays.

item.title: Main slick contained, Unified Command says; about 142,000 gallons of oil-water mix recovered
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Primary skimming is finished and the response is shifting to shoreline cleanup. Fishing and shellfish closures in both bays stay in place pending state testing.
item.content:encoded:
The main oil slick from the Inner Harbor discharge is contained, the Unified Command said Monday, three weeks after crude from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

Recovery. Primary skimming operations have concluded with about 142,000 gallons of oil-water mixture recovered. The figure is for mixed oil and water as collected, not for oil alone. The release has been estimated at about 9,000 barrels of crude.

Water quality. State monitoring readings in Corpus Christi Bay have fallen to an average of 0.40 milligrams per liter of petroleum hydrocarbons, down from a peak of 3.4 recorded Sept. 17, the update said. The raw water intake at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant is back below its 0.10 milligram-per-liter alert threshold.

Wildlife. Coastal Bend Wildlife Rescue has documented 340 oiled birds; 198 have been rehabilitated and released.

Shoreline. Hand crews are working about 6.4 kilometers of affected shoreline in Nueces Bay. The response is moving from emergency containment to shoreline cleanup.

Closures. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in both bays remain closed pending state testing.

"Contained means the slick is no longer spreading. It does not mean the shoreline is clean, and it does not reopen the bays," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "The work now is slower. It is people with hand tools on marsh edges."

Operator notes. Containment is one condition for moving ships through the inner channel again, but not the only one. The Coast Guard has not set a reopening date for the ship channel, which has been closed since Sept. 13. Both tankers remain at the Rendal Terminals berth, and the investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to their cargo-control systems is open.

item.title: Federal authorities examining pre-storm drone flights over port and a utility site, sources say
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Sources familiar with the investigation say commercial drones may have flown over the Port of Corpus Christi and at least one power utility facility in the week before Rafael. The FBI is asking for tips.
item.content:encoded:
Federal authorities are examining whether commercial drones conducted surveillance flights over the Port of Corpus Christi and at least one local power utility facility in the days before Hurricane Rafael, sources familiar with the investigation told Gulfwater.

What the sources say. The flights took place in the week before landfall. They were detected through radar records maintained by the Coast Guard. No organization has claimed responsibility.

Why investigators care. The timing has drawn attention because of the damage to critical infrastructure during and after the storm, the sources said. They did not say that the flights caused any of it, and Gulfwater has no information that they did.

On the record. The Federal Aviation Administration and Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations confirmed Wednesday that investigators had identified multiple incidents of unauthorized unmanned aircraft operations in the Corpus Christi area in the period before the storm. The agencies said the aircraft flew without required authorizations and were detected through radar and electronic sensor records. They released no numbers, locations or times.

"We can confirm the FBI is investigating reports of unauthorized drone activity in the Corpus Christi area," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "Anyone with information should contact the FBI. We have no further comment."

The Coast Guard declined to discuss the radar records.

Port condition. Unchanged. The ship channel remains closed to all traffic while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor spill is contained.

Not known. Who operated the aircraft. How many flights there were. Which port and utility sites were overflown. Whether the flights are connected to any other matter under investigation.

Operator notes. Terminal security officers who logged drone sightings in early September should preserve camera footage and gate records and report them to the FBI. Gulfwater does not speculate on attribution and will report findings as agencies release them.

item.title: Held at the berth: what a Captain of the Port order means for Kalvora Star and Ostrel Bay
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Ten days after the Coast Guard said neither tanker would move, both remain alongside at Rendal Terminals. An explainer on the authority involved and what usually has to happen before a held ship sails.
item.content:encoded:
MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay have not moved since before Hurricane Rafael. On Sept. 20 the Coast Guard said both would stay moored at the Rendal Terminals berth under a Captain of the Port order until the investigation into the Inner Harbor oil release, and the owners' obligations under federal oil spill law, are addressed. Ten days later, both are still there. Here is what that status means.

The authority. A Captain of the Port can direct the movement of any vessel in the port when safety, security or the environment requires it. An order can keep a ship at a berth, send it to an anchorage or set conditions for sailing. It stays in force until the Captain of the Port lifts it.

Why these ships. The Unified Command has attributed an estimated 9,000 barrels of spilled crude to the two tankers. Investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to their cargo-control systems, and Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains tanker cargo systems, has said its remote-maintenance credentials were misused. The ships are both the source of the spill and the place investigators have to work.

What usually has to happen. In general terms, three things stand between a held tanker and departure: investigators finish what they need aboard; the vessel is shown to be safe to move, cargo systems included; and the owner's financial responsibilities for the spill are in order. The Coast Guard designated both owners as responsible parties on Sept. 21. A claims center run for the owners opened Sunday.

"I can tell you the order is in effect and both vessels are where they were," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "I can't give you a date, and I won't discuss the investigation."

A maritime security analyst who is not involved in the case said the length of the hold is not unusual on its own. "When the question is what happened inside a ship's systems, the ship is the evidence," he said. "Nobody releases the evidence early."

Operator notes. Both tankers were laden when the storm arrived. Whether remaining cargo is discharged before either ship moves, and under what supervision, has not been addressed publicly. The ship channel remains closed to all traffic.

item.title: Corpus Christi channel closure enters third week as spill response works the Inner Harbor
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The Coast Guard has not set a reopening date. The investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to two tankers' cargo systems continues.
item.content:encoded:
Port status, Sept. 27: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed to traffic. Crude exports halted. No reopening date announced.

The port has been closed to inbound traffic since Sept. 12, when 14 vessels were holding at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, and the channel to all traffic since Sept. 13. Ships that put to sea for Hurricane Rafael have been back at the anchorage since Sept. 17. The closure is now in its third week. The port is estimated to handle about half of U.S. crude exports.

"The channel will reopen when it is safe for vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "That determination depends on conditions in the waterway, including the ongoing spill response. We will announce changes to port conditions as they are made."

Spill response: The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor as the storm arrived. Surge and wind carried oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, with sheen over about 33 square miles. Boom deployment began as winds dropped. The Unified Command requested Navy salvage equipment early in the response.

Investigation: The Coast Guard said Sept. 20 that investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers' cargo-control systems, with federal cyber teams assisting. On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a cargo-systems maintenance vendor, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access. Ruiz said there was nothing new to report. "When there is information we can release, we will release it," she said.

Watch items: Ruiz did not comment on vessel counts at the anchorage or on the order in which vessels will be allowed in once the channel reopens. Gulfwater will track port condition changes as they are announced.

item.title: Spill claims center opens for the tankers' owners, as federal oil spill law requires
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The center takes claims for cleanup costs and property damage from the Inner Harbor spill. Claimants should bring records, and the bays remain closed to fishing.
item.content:encoded:
A claims center run for the owners of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay opened Sunday for cleanup and property damage claims from the Inner Harbor oil spill. Federal oil spill law requires responsible parties to provide a claims process; the Coast Guard designated the two tankers' owners on Tuesday.

What it takes. The center's opening notice covers spill cleanup costs and property damage. It does not address lost income.

Who should file. Shoreline property owners with oiled docks, bulkheads, boats or gear, and anyone who paid out of pocket to clean oil from property.

What to bring. Dated photographs, receipts, proof of ownership, and a description of where and when the oil arrived.

"If oil from this spill damaged your property or you paid to clean it up, file," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Bring photographs and receipts. Keep copies of everything you hand over."

The backstop. The Coast Guard opened the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund last week with an initial ceiling of $4.2 million so that response work would not wait on the owners. The fund's costs are to be recovered from the responsible parties.

Fishers. Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed to fishing and shellfish harvesting since Sept. 18. Whitaker said fishers should keep trip logs, landing records and expense records for as long as the closures last.

Status. The release is estimated at about 9,000 barrels. The cause remains under investigation: the Coast Guard has said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems, and Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains tanker cargo systems, has said its remote-maintenance credentials were misused. The ship channel remains closed, and both tankers remain at the Rendal Terminals berth.

Gulfwater will report any change in what the center accepts.

item.title: Ten days shut: what has to be checked before Corpus Christi's channel can reopen
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Depths, buoys, debris and oil. A working list of what stands between the offshore anchorage and the docks, and why nobody is offering a date.
item.content:encoded:
Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: closed to all traffic for the 12th day. Ships that rode out Hurricane Rafael at sea remain at the offshore anchorage. No reopening date has been issued.

Gulfwater asked what has to be true before deep-draft ships move again. The working list:

Depths. A hurricane moves sediment. Rafael pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and the dredged channel is the deepest water in a shallow system.

"A surge like that rearranges a shallow bay," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi who models storm surge. "I would not assume the bottom is where the chart says until someone has measured it."

Aids to navigation. Buoys can drag off station and range lights can be damaged. Pilots need them verified before taking a loaded tanker through the jetties.

Obstructions. Debris, sunken small craft and anything torn loose from shore have to be found and marked or removed.

Oil. This is the item that makes Corpus Christi different from an ordinary storm closure. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill was carried into both bays, and state agencies have closed fishing and shellfish harvesting there. Boom and response vessels are working in and near the channel, and ships cannot move through that work.

"Reopening comes in stages, and the survey sets the pace," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The spill response is part of that picture. We will announce each stage when it is ready and not before."

What operators can do now. Keep ships at the anchorage ready to move on short notice. Expect draft or daylight limits on the first transits. Expect the order of arrivals to be set with the pilots, not by time at anchor alone. Ask terminals at the Inner Harbor what conditions they will set near the spill site.

item.title: Brightwake chief: remote access stays off until customers can trust it
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The cargo-systems maintenance vendor says it does not know who misused its credentials and will not discuss specific vessels while the investigation is open.
item.content:encoded:
Brightwake Marine Systems, the vendor that said Wednesday its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, will keep all remote access to customer systems switched off until it can show customers a safer way to connect, its chief executive said Thursday.

"I don't know who did this, and I'm not going to guess," Owen Pryce told Gulfwater Maritime Report. "I want to know as badly as anyone. Right now my job is to make sure it can't happen again through us."

Brightwake supports cargo-control systems aboard tankers, the shipboard software and hardware crews use to monitor and manage cargo. Like most marine system vendors, it has provided remote support, connecting from shore to diagnose faults and install updates rather than sending a technician aboard for every job.

Pryce said the company revoked all remote access across its customer base. He described changes Brightwake intends to make before restoring any connection: sessions scheduled in advance, approved by the crew on board, watched in real time from the vessel and closed when the work is done. "No standing access, and every session approved by someone on board," he said. "That's where we're going."

He declined to say which vessels or operators use Brightwake systems. "I won't discuss specific vessels while the investigation is open," he said.

Status: Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said Monday that investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth involved in the release of about 9,000 barrels of crude during Hurricane Rafael. Federal cyber teams are assisting. The Coast Guard has not publicly linked any company to the investigation. Asked about Brightwake's statement, Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz said the investigation continues and the Coast Guard would not characterize any party's role.

Port conditions: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed to all traffic since Sept. 13. Crude exports halted. No reopening date announced.

item.title: Coast Guard designates owners of Kalvora Star and Ostrel Bay as responsible parties; trust fund opened at $4.2 million
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Oil fingerprinting matched samples from the Inner Harbor and both bays to the two tankers' cargoes. The designation assigns the bill for the response. It is not a finding on cause.
item.content:encoded:
The Coast Guard on Tuesday formally designated the owners of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay as responsible parties for the Inner Harbor oil release under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.

Basis. Oil fingerprint analysis by the Coast Guard matched samples collected in the Inner Harbor, Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay to the crude cargoes aboard the two vessels, the Federal On-Scene Coordinator said. The discharge estimate is unchanged at about 9,000 barrels.

Obligations. The owners have been issued Notices of Federal Interest. They are required to fund cleanup and to set up a process for damage claims.

Trust fund. To keep response contractors working without interruption, the Coast Guard opened the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund with an initial ceiling of $4.2 million. That money is to be recovered from the responsible parties.

What it is not. The designation assigns financial responsibility for the response. It is not a finding on the cause of the release, which remains under investigation. On Monday the Coast Guard said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems.

"This step is about who pays for the response, and the law is clear on that," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "How the oil came to be released is a separate question, and that investigation is open."

Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said the state's advice to people with losses has not changed. "Keep records now. A claims process has to be set up, and when it is, documentation is everything," he said.

Operator notes. For owners and charterers the designation follows the statute: liability for removal costs and damages attaches to the vessel interests first, whatever the eventual finding on cause. The Unified Command has not publicly identified either owner by name. Both tankers remain held at the Rendal Terminals berth, and the ship channel remains closed.

item.title: Coast Guard files Rafael SAR summary: 341 hoists, 1,041 surface rescues; after-action review due in 90 days
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Sector Corpus Christi's incident summary report certifies 1,427 rescues and credits contracted drone operators with 112 thermal annotations used by surface craft.
item.content:encoded:
Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi has filed its formal Incident Summary Report for the Hurricane Rafael search and rescue operation with Coast Guard District 8, the sector said Tuesday. The report, ISR-2027-CC-004, certifies 1,427 total rescues.

Breakdown as certified: 341 by helicopter hoist; 1,041 by surface vessel, a category that covers Coast Guard, state and civilian craft; and 45 ambulatory survivor contacts, meaning people who were found and assisted but did not need to be lifted or carried out.

The surface figure is the one of interest to the working waterfront. Nearly three of every four rescues were made from the water, in flooded streets and along the bay shore, not from the air. County officials said Sunday that 87 credentialed civilian boat operators worked alongside the official teams, and that 34 teams were coordinated at the peak of the operation.

The report also notes that contracted unmanned aircraft operators provided 112 thermal imaging annotations that were used directly to coordinate surface rescues. In practice that means a marked position passed from an aircraft to a boat crew.

Timeline from Coast Guard and county statements: helicopter operations began at 1:22 a.m. Tuesday, Sept. 14. By 3 p.m. Wednesday, Sept. 15, crews had completed 180 hoists and all rescues by air stood at 341, with 486 people reached in total. The cumulative count was 702 on Thursday evening and 1,427 when mass rescue operations concluded Sunday, Sept. 19.

Channel status is unchanged. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed to all traffic since Port Condition Zulu was set at noon on Monday, Sept. 13, and remains closed for damage surveys and for the oil spill response in the Inner Harbor. Rescue craft operated inside the bays under Coast Guard direction; no commercial movements have resumed.

A formal after-action review of the SAR operation will be conducted within 90 days, the Coast Guard said. For operators, the items to watch in that review are how civilian vessels were credentialed and tasked, how positions were passed between aircraft, drones and boats, and whether those arrangements are written into the area's contingency plans before next season.

The Coast Guard thanked the community and its mutual-aid partners for their response.

item.title: Coast Guard completes inspections aboard Kalvora Star and Ostrel Bay; both tankers held at berth
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Marine inspectors and pollution investigators finished aboard both ships Sunday. Crews are safe, and neither vessel moves until the investigation and the owners' spill obligations are addressed.
item.content:encoded:
Coast Guard marine inspectors and pollution investigators completed inspections Sunday aboard MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released as Hurricane Rafael arrived, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said Monday.

Crews. Both crews are safe, the sector said.

Vessel status. Both tankers remain moored at the berth under a Captain of the Port order. Neither will move until the investigation and the owners' obligations under federal oil spill law are addressed. The sector gave no timeline.

Scope. Investigators documented the condition of the cargo systems on both ships. The statement repeats what the Coast Guard disclosed earlier Monday: investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems, with federal cyber teams assisting. The Coast Guard said it will not characterize the cause of the release while the investigation is open.

"The inspections are complete, the vessels are staying where they are, and the cause is not something I can discuss," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, the sector's public affairs officer.

Rendal Terminals said it is cooperating. "We are cooperating fully with the Unified Command and with investigators," said Victor Lang, a company spokesperson.

Response. Containment boom is deployed along affected shoreline in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in both bays have been closed since Saturday.

Operator notes. Two loaded tankers held at an Inner Harbor berth, with a safety zone around them, are now fixed features of any reopening plan. Deep-draft traffic to berths farther up the Inner Harbor has to pass them. The Coast Guard has not said how it will sequence that, and the channel remains closed to all traffic. The formal responsible-party designation the Unified Command said to expect has not yet been issued.

item.title: Coast Guard examining possible unauthorized remote access to spill tankers' cargo systems
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Investigators are looking at the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers at the center of the Inner Harbor spill. Federal cyber teams are assisting.
item.content:encoded:
Investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of the two crude tankers involved in the Inner Harbor spill, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said Monday. Federal cyber teams are assisting.

MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay were moored laden at the Rendal Terminals berth with Coast Guard approval when Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island early Sept. 14. Oil was reported spilling at the berth as the storm arrived. The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office estimates the release at about 9,000 barrels of crude.

"Investigators are examining the possibility of unauthorized remote access to the vessels' cargo-control systems, and federal cyber teams are supporting that work," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Sector Corpus Christi public affairs officer. "We will not characterize the cause of the discharge until the investigation supports a conclusion."

Until Monday the cause had been described only as under investigation. Ruiz did not say which onboard systems were being examined, what type of access was involved or whether any other vessels were affected.

Cargo-control systems on modern tankers monitor and manage cargo handling, including tank levels and pumps during loading and discharge. Many operators allow approved technicians to connect to those systems from shore for maintenance and software support.

Rendal Terminals, which operates the berth, said it is cooperating. "Rendal Terminals is cooperating fully with the Unified Command and with federal investigators," spokesman Victor Lang said. "We will not comment on the substance of an active investigation."

Port conditions: The port has been closed to inbound traffic since Sept. 12, when crude exports halted, and the ship channel to all traffic since Sept. 13. Vessels that put to sea for the storm are back at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas. The Coast Guard has not announced a reopening date. The Unified Command requested Navy salvage equipment early in the response, and crews began deploying boom once winds dropped.

item.title: Unified Command: heavy oiling on Nueces Bay shoreline; fishing and shellfish harvesting closed in both bays
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Forty-one oiled birds have been documented. More boom is going in at the Nueces Bay Causeway channel, and the Coast Guard expects to designate responsible parties within 72 hours.
item.content:encoded:
Status, Saturday evening: ship channel closed; safety zone in the Inner Harbor; Nueces and Corpus Christi bays closed to fishing and shellfish harvesting.

The Unified Command for the Inner Harbor oil spill said Saturday that crude released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay has heavily oiled parts of the Nueces Bay shoreline. Sheen covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, unchanged from Thursday's estimate.

Water. A Texas Commission on Environmental Quality monitoring station in Nueces Bay recorded petroleum hydrocarbons at 2.1 milligrams per liter Saturday afternoon, the update said.

Wildlife. Texas Parks and Wildlife biologists and Coastal Bend Wildlife Rescue have documented 41 oiled birds along the Nueces Bay shoreline, including brown pelicans and laughing gulls. Rescue operations are under way.

Closures. Because of the oil, Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in both bays, effective immediately and until further notice.

Boom. Additional containment boom is being placed at the Nueces Bay Causeway channel.

Responsible party. The Coast Guard expects to issue its formal designation within 72 hours, the update said. The Unified Command has put the release at about 9,000 barrels. The cause remains under investigation.

"The closures follow the oil. They stay until testing says the water and the catch are clean," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "People who fish these bays for a living should start keeping records of what this costs them."

Operator notes. Nothing in Saturday's update changes port status. The channel has been shut since Monday, and the ships that rode out the storm at sea are back at the offshore anchorage, waiting. Response craft are working the Inner Harbor and the bay reach of the channel, and any reopening plan will have to account for them.

item.title: Relief cargo waits on closed Corpus Christi channel as spill response continues
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Forty relief containers booked on MV Gulf Provider before Rafael can't move until the port reopens. The anchorage queue remains held.
item.content:encoded:
Forty containers of relief supplies booked on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider before Hurricane Rafael remain undelivered with the Port of Corpus Christi still closed to traffic, five days after Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi shut the ship channel to all traffic.

"The boxes are booked, the paperwork's clean, and none of it matters until I've got water to bring a ship through," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, the freight forwarder handling the shipment. "Every day the channel's shut is a day those supplies aren't on a truck to somebody who needs them."

Relief agencies stocked warehouses ahead of peak season and forwarders signed standby relief contracts over the summer, Akins noted, but the booked containers were meant to restock those shelves after a storm.

Anchorage: Ships that rode out the storm at sea have been returning since Friday to the anchorage east of Port Aransas to wait for the channel. Count at the Sept. 12 inbound closure: 14 vessels. No reopening timeline has been issued.

"Reopening the channel is a safety decision," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, the sector's public affairs officer. "It will happen when the waterway is safe for traffic and for the response, and not before."

Inside the port, the Unified Command led by the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office continues to respond to the release of about 9,000 barrels of crude from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor. Oil carried by surge and wind covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Boom deployment began Thursday, and the Texas Department of State Health Services and Texas Parks and Wildlife shut shellfish harvesting and fishing in both bays Saturday. Navy salvage equipment has been requested. Cause is under investigation.

Akins said his company was looking at whether any supplies could move overland in the meantime. "In this business you always have a plan B," he said. "Plan B for forty boxes on a ship is a lot of trucks I don't have."

Gulfwater will report channel status and anchorage changes as the sector releases them.

item.title: Who pays for the Inner Harbor spill: how federal oil spill law will sort it out
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: No responsible party has been formally designated yet. Here is how the Oil Pollution Act process works, what the Unified Command has said so far, and what fishers and shoreline owners can do in the meantime.
item.content:encoded:
Four days after crude from two tankers spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, shoreline owners and fishers are asking who pays. The answer runs through the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, the federal law that governs oil spills from vessels. This is how the process works and where the Corpus Christi response stands.

Where it stands. The Unified Command of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office has put the release at about 9,000 barrels from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth. Sheen has covered about 33 square miles of the two bays. The cause is under investigation. As of Saturday morning, the Coast Guard had not issued a formal responsible-party designation.

Step one: designation. Under the act, the Coast Guard's Federal On-Scene Coordinator designates the responsible party for a discharge from a vessel, normally its owner or operator. Designation settles who funds the response. It is not a finding of fault or cause.

Step two: funding. A designated party pays for cleanup. If payment lags, the Coast Guard can draw on the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund to keep contractors working and recover the money later.

Step three: claims. A designated party must set up and advertise a way to file claims for cleanup costs and damages. A claim that is denied, or that sits unanswered for 90 days, can be taken to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

"Nobody needs to wait for a form to start keeping records," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the General Land Office's oil spill program. "Photograph the shoreline. Keep trip logs and receipts. Write down dates. When a claims process is announced, that file is what you will need."

What to watch. The designation itself; any announcement of a claims process; and state decisions on fishing and shellfish harvesting in the oiled bays, which would bear directly on what fishers can claim.

Gulfwater will report each step as it is announced.

item.title: Storm-riding ships return to Corpus Christi anchorage; channel stays shut for survey and spill work
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Vessels that put to sea ahead of Rafael are back offshore and waiting. Two jobs stand between them and the docks: a channel survey and containment of the Inner Harbor spill.
item.content:encoded:
Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: closed to all traffic. No reopening date issued.

Offshore. Ships that put to sea ahead of Hurricane Rafael have returned to the offshore anchorage to wait. The anchorage is refilling with the same vessels that left it Monday.

Why the channel is still shut. Two jobs come first. The channel has to be surveyed after the storm. And the spill at the Inner Harbor has to be contained.

"The channel will reopen when it has been surveyed and the spill response allows it," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are not going to give a date we cannot keep. Vessels at the anchorage should stay in contact with their agents and wait for notice."

The spill. The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth. Surge and wind carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Sheen covers about 33 square miles, with oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in marshes. Crews began deploying boom as the winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline is open.

The port. "We are assessing our facilities and supporting the Unified Command," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The channel reopens on the Coast Guard's decision. We will be ready to work when it does."

What a reopening usually looks like. Restrictions are lifted in stages, with draft limits or daylight-only transits first. With oil in the channel, operators should also expect conditions tied to the spill response.

Operator notes. Keep clear of the entrance and of response vessels working the bays. Confirm that agents have current positions and readiness. Do not plan on rumor. Gulfwater will report each change in port condition as it is issued.

item.title: Rafael surge carried Inner Harbor crude into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays; boom deployed as winds ease
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The Unified Command reports sheen over about 33 square miles after the release from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. Navy salvage equipment has been requested. The port remains closed.
item.content:encoded:
Crude released from two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth on Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor has moved out of the ship channel and into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, carried by Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind, the Unified Command said Thursday. Sheen covers about 33 square miles.

The Unified Command, formed Wednesday by Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office, estimates the release from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at about 9,000 barrels. Oil has reached shorelines at North Beach and Portland and marshes in Nueces Bay.

Responders began deploying containment boom Thursday as winds dropped. On-water operations had been held since the storm because of conditions. The Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment; type and arrival time were not specified.

Boom placement in the first days of a spill typically prioritizes sensitive habitat and water intakes over open water, and shallow bay depths limit where larger response vessels can operate.

"Our crews are on the water now that conditions allow it," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, the sector's public affairs officer. "Shoreline protection is the priority. The cause of the release remains under investigation, and we will not speculate on it."

The Coast Guard had approved both tankers staying alongside through the storm when it closed the channel to all traffic Monday. The Unified Command has not released details on the vessels' owners, flags or cargo grades.

The port remains closed to traffic. The 14 vessels that held at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas before the storm put to sea Monday to ride it out. No reopening timeline has been issued. Spill response will shape when and how vessels can transit oiled water in the inner channel, on top of the post-storm surveys a reopening normally requires.

Gulfwater will report Unified Command operational updates, channel status and anchorage counts as they are released.

item.title: Coast Guard confirms Inner Harbor crude has reached both bays; safety zone set, boom going out as winds drop
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Morning overflights show sheen across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The source remains the two tankers named Wednesday. A wildlife hotline is open.
item.content:encoded:
Status, Thursday morning: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed. Safety zone in effect in the Inner Harbor. Sheen in Nueces Bay and Corpus Christi Bay.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi confirmed Thursday that crude oil released at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived has moved out of the ship channel and into both bays. Coast Guard overflights and NOAA aerial imagery taken Thursday morning show sheen across about 33 square miles, with oil on shorelines and in marshes, the sector said in a statement.

Source. The Coast Guard said the oil came from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers the Unified Command named Wednesday. The release estimate is unchanged at about 9,000 barrels. The cause is under investigation.

Response. With winds dropping, crews began deploying containment boom Thursday. A wildlife hotline has opened for reports of oiled animals. The National Response Center has been notified.

Restrictions. The Captain of the Port has established a safety zone in the Inner Harbor. The channel remains closed to all traffic, as it has been since Port Condition Zulu was set Monday. The Coast Guard advised the public to avoid contact with oil and oiled shoreline and to stay out of affected waters.

"Surge and wind did the moving. The oil left the channel with the water," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, which shares the Unified Command with the Coast Guard. "Now that the wind is down, boom goes where it protects the most shoreline first."

Operator notes. The safety zone and the spill response add a second condition to any reopening. Beyond the standard post-storm survey of depths and aids to navigation, vessels bound for inner berths will have to transit water that response craft are working. Ships that put to sea Monday have been given no date for the channel.

Gulfwater will carry the Unified Command's afternoon update.

item.title: Unified Command: about 9,000 barrels released from two tankers at Rendal Terminals berth
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office name MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. On-water response is waiting for the wind to drop, and Navy salvage equipment has been requested.
item.content:encoded:
An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office said Wednesday.

Command. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Land Office have formed a Unified Command to run the response.

Vessels. The tankers are MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. They are the two laden ships that remained moored at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval when the port went to Condition Zulu on Monday.

Cause. Under investigation. Oil was reported spilling at the terminal as the storm came in. Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane.

"The estimate is about 9,000 barrels and it is an estimate," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The cause is under investigation and we will not speculate."

Response. On-water work is waiting for winds to drop. The Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment.

"As soon as the wind lets us, boom goes in the water," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Land Office's oil spill program. "Until then our crews are staging equipment and checking shoreline where it is safe to do so."

Terminal. "Rendal Terminals is cooperating fully with the Unified Command," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. "We will not comment on the cause while the investigation is under way."

Port condition. Closed to all traffic. Ships that left the offshore anchorage to ride out the storm remain at sea.

Not yet known. How the oil left the ships. The condition of the vessels and the berth. How far surge and wind have carried oil beyond the Inner Harbor. When the channel can be surveyed.

Operator notes. Do not approach the entrance. Await Coast Guard notices. Operators with ships due at Inner Harbor berths should expect delays that go beyond the storm closure itself.

item.title: Corpus Christi port stays shut after Rafael landfall; discharge reported at Inner Harbor crude berth
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The ship channel remains closed, and ships from the offshore anchorage are still at sea. The Coast Guard reports a discharge from two laden tankers that stayed alongside through the storm.
item.content:encoded:
The Port of Corpus Christi remained closed to vessel traffic Tuesday after Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island at about 0100 local as a Category 3 storm. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi closed the port to inbound traffic Sunday, with 14 vessels holding at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, and closed the channel to all traffic Monday, when those ships put to sea.

The sector reported a discharge from two laden tankers moored at a crude terminal on the Inner Harbor. Both had remained alongside through the storm with Coast Guard approval after the channel closed. Keeping laden tonnage at a protected berth rather than sailing it ahead of a storm is decided case by case with the Captain of the Port. The sector did not identify the vessels or the terminal operator.

Volume is unknown. Cause is under investigation. "We cannot put responders on the water in these conditions," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, the sector's public affairs officer.

The National Weather Service estimates surge of about 11 feet entered Corpus Christi and Nueces bays at landfall. Winds remained strong at midday. Containment boom is of limited use in high winds and steep chop, and on-water spill operations generally wait until conditions ease.

Reopening a channel after a storm of this strength typically requires hydrographic surveys for shoaling and obstructions, checks of aids to navigation and an assessment of terminal and dock damage before the Captain of the Port lifts restrictions. The sector has given no timeline.

Crude exports, about half of the U.S. total by analysts' estimates, have been halted since Sunday. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement through the port, a strategic military seaport, was postponed Saturday.

Gulfwater will report channel status, anchorage counts and spill response details, including vessel identities, as the sector releases them.

item.title: Port Condition Zulu: Corpus Christi ship channel shut to all traffic; anchorage empties as Rafael closes in
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The Captain of the Port set Zulu at noon Monday. Ships that had been holding offshore were ordered to sea, and two laden tankers are staying at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval.
item.content:encoded:
Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Monday evening: closed to all traffic. The Coast Guard Captain of the Port set Port Condition Zulu at noon, the last step in a three-day sequence that began with X-Ray on Saturday and closed the port to inbound vessels under Yankee on Sunday.

Under Zulu, no commercial vessel moves in the port or its approaches. Ships that had been holding at the offshore anchorage since Sunday were directed to put to sea and ride out Hurricane Rafael with sea room. The joint notice from the Port of Corpus Christi Authority and the Coast Guard gave them until 6 p.m. to clear the anchorage. By early evening the anchorage was empty.

Exceptions. Two laden tankers are staying alongside at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval. The Coast Guard did not name the vessels or the terminal.

"Zulu means the channel is shut. No inbound, no outbound, no shifting between berths," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Vessels that were at anchor are heading for sea room. The two ships remaining alongside have Coast Guard approval to stay."

Terminals have stopped work. "Cargo operations are secured and non-essential people have gone home," said Javier Salinas, spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Nothing restarts until the Coast Guard has surveyed the channel and we have inspected the docks."

Operator notes. Crude loading stopped Sunday when the port closed to inbound traffic; 14 inbound vessels were waiting offshore at that point, and all have now been ordered to sea. Reopening follows the usual order: a Coast Guard survey of channel depth and aids to navigation, then terminal inspections, then traffic by priority. No timeline has been given.

Forecast. Rafael, a Category 3 hurricane, is forecast to come ashore near Port Aransas overnight with 9 to 12 feet of surge. Gulfwater will report port conditions as the Coast Guard changes them.

item.title: Port Condition Yankee: Corpus Christi closed to inbound traffic; 14 vessels hold at offshore anchorage
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Crude exports halt and ocean-going ships head out as Hurricane Rafael nears. The Coast Guard has not said when the port will reopen.
item.content:encoded:
Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi set Port Condition Yankee for the Port of Corpus Christi on Sunday, closing the port to inbound traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Ocean-going ships in port are heading out. Fourteen inbound vessels are holding at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, and crude exports have halted.

"The port is closed to inbound vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector spokeswoman. "Departing vessels should coordinate their transits with the Captain of the Port and the pilots. We will announce any further change in port condition through broadcast notices."

Yankee tightens Saturday's Port Condition X-Ray, under which the port stayed open while ships made departure plans and terminals wound down crude loading. Port conditions step up as the forecast arrival of gale-force winds draws closer.

Status, Sunday evening: Inbound transits suspended. Outbound departures of ocean-going ships under way. Crude loadings halted. Anchorage count: 14 inbound vessels.

Vessels at the anchorage remain under Coast Guard direction. In heavy weather, ships at anchor commonly put to sea, where they have room to maneuver; Ruiz would not say what the sector expects of them as the storm nears.

"Our terminals have stopped loading, and crews are securing the docks," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Everything we do today is about getting through the storm and being ready to restart after it."

Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, by analysts' estimates, so the halt reaches well beyond the Coastal Bend. The 40 relief containers booked on MV Gulf Provider are also on hold.

Forecasters issued a hurricane warning for the Coastal Bend on Sunday afternoon and expect Rafael to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm.

Gulfwater will track the anchorage and the next port condition change.

item.title: Coast Guard sets Port Condition YANKEE at Corpus Christi; inbound traffic halted, deep-draft vessels ordered to sea
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The Captain of the Port Corpus Christi set Port Condition YANKEE Sunday morning, closing the port to all inbound traffic and directing ocean-going vessels at berth to depart for open-sea anchorage.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The U.S. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi set Port Condition YANKEE Sunday morning as Hurricane Rafael approaches the Texas coast, formally closing the Port of Corpus Christi to inbound vessel traffic and triggering the departure of deep-draft vessels from their berths in the ship channel.

Captain of the Port Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han issued the YANKEE condition at 0930 local time, signaling that hazardous conditions are anticipated within 24 hours. Under YANKEE protocols, all vessels with the ability to safely get underway are expected to depart and seek sea room well outside the forecast cone. Ocean-going tankers, bulk carriers, and container ships that had been working cargo at the La Quinta Channel berths and the bulk facilities along the Inner Harbor began standby procedures for departure through the morning and early afternoon hours.

"Our priority at this stage is to get deep-draft traffic out of the channel and clear the port for storm conditions," Ostrowski-Han said in a statement released through Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Vessel operators who can safely transit to offshore anchorage should do so without delay. Those with mechanical limitations or crew deficiencies need to contact the Vessel Traffic Service immediately so we can assist with coordination."

Port of Corpus Christi Authority Director of Operations Julio Sandoval-Reeves confirmed that the port's industrial terminals are following shutdown protocols in coordination with the Coast Guard. Petroleum product loading operations at the Inner Harbor oil docks were halted by midday Sunday, with terminal operators securing hoses, vapor lines, and shore connections ahead of the storm. The La Quinta Channel, which handles LNG and bulk cargo on the north side of the bay, was placed on reduced operations as remaining vessels received orders to depart.

Vessel Traffic Service Corpus Christi is monitoring marine traffic and coordinating departures through Channel 16 and 22A. The Coast Guard anticipates escalating to Port Condition ZULU — full closure — within 24 hours depending on Rafael's track and intensity. Mariners are reminded that YANKEE conditions mean the window for orderly departure is closing rapidly.

item.title: Coast Guard sets Port Condition X-Ray for Corpus Christi; ocean-going ships told to plan departures
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The port stays open, but gale-force winds from Hurricane Rafael are possible within 48 hours. Terminals are winding down crude loading, and ships must leave or get Coast Guard approval to stay.
item.content:encoded:
Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi set Port Condition X-Ray for the Port of Corpus Christi on Saturday ahead of Hurricane Rafael, meaning gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. The port remains open. Ocean-going vessels must plan to depart or obtain Coast Guard approval to remain, and crude terminals have begun winding down loading.

"The Port of Corpus Christi remains open under Port Condition X-Ray, and ocean-going vessels should finalize departure plans now or request approval to remain," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Mariners should monitor Coast Guard broadcast notices and port channels for any change in port status."

X-Ray is one step in a graduated series of storm port conditions. Tighter conditions can follow as the storm nears, and vessels at the offshore anchorage remain subject to Coast Guard direction.

Requests to remain in port go to the Captain of the Port, Ruiz said. She did not say whether any vessel had applied. "Vessels remaining in port do so with Coast Guard approval and under conditions set for that approval," Ruiz said. She declined to describe those conditions.

The storm is also affecting military cargo. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement through Corpus Christi has been postponed, Army officials said. The port is a designated strategic seaport, and the brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer.

Rafael's forecast cone has covered Corpus Christi since Thursday. Relief cargo booked ahead of the storm, including 40 containers on MV Gulf Provider, could be caught by any closure.

Ruiz would not speculate on whether the port will close. Reopening after any storm closure generally depends on conditions easing, on surveys of the channel for shoaling and obstructions, and on the status of aids to navigation and port facilities.

"We set port conditions on the forecast and on what is safe," she said.

Gulfwater will report the anchorage count and any change in port status as the Coast Guard announces them.

item.title: Rafael's cone covers Corpus Christi; no port condition set, operators start the clock anyway
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The port is open and no watches are posted. Relief shipments are already booked, including 40 containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider.
item.content:encoded:
Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Thursday afternoon: open to all traffic. No hurricane port condition has been set. No watches are posted for the Texas coast.

The storm. Hurricane Rafael is over the southern Gulf after crossing the Yucatan Peninsula, and forecasters have warned it could strengthen over warm water. The forecast cone shifted toward the Texas coast and now covers Corpus Christi. Officials are urging residents to prepare.

What that means on the water today. Nothing has been ordered. Loadings continue, and tankers remain at the offshore anchorage. But the cone is the signal most heavy-weather plans use to start counting backward.

"Nothing has changed in port status today," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "We are in close contact with the Coast Guard. Customers should watch for the Captain of the Port's notices and should not wait on us to review their own plans."

Relief cargo. Relief shipments were being booked before any watch. They include 40 containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider, arranged by the freight forwarder Gulf Relief Logistics under the standby contracts Gulfwater described in August.

"We booked the boxes on the Gulf Provider this week," said Terry Akins, the company's regional manager. "If the storm goes somewhere else, that cargo follows it. If it comes here, the ship will be waiting for the channel like everybody else."

Operator notes. Ships at the berth: confirm with terminals how long a safe cargo shutdown takes. Ships at anchor: check engine readiness and stores now. Operators who may ask to remain in port should have the mooring plan ready to file. Agents should confirm pilot and tug availability for an early departure queue.

Gulfwater will report any change in port condition as soon as it is issued.

item.title: Tanker operators track Rafael as Corpus Christi anchorage holds steady
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: The ship channel remains open with tankers queued offshore. A look at what port status changes would mean for vessels at anchor and alongside if Rafael's track holds toward Texas.
item.content:encoded:
Tropical Storm Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean on Saturday, with early forecasts showing a west-northwest track over the Yucatan Peninsula and into the Gulf toward Texas. As of Monday, the Corpus Christi Ship Channel remained open, and crude tankers continued to wait at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas.

The traffic picture is the one Gulfwater has described all summer. Corpus Christi crude exports hit a monthly high in August, and the port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analysts. The anchorage has functioned as the buffer between arrivals and berth availability.

A tropical system changes that calculation in stages. The Coast Guard sets port conditions based on when gale-force winds are expected to arrive. As conditions tighten, inbound traffic can be suspended and the channel can be closed to all vessel movements. Vessels at anchor commonly weigh anchor and put to sea to ride out heavy weather away from the coast, where they have room to maneuver. Oceangoing vessels already in port may be required to depart before the closure or to request permission to remain.

Vessels remaining in port during a storm typically do so under conditions set by the captain of the port, which can cover mooring arrangements, crewing and readiness to get under way. Those decisions are made vessel by vessel.

Operators also plan for the other side of a storm. When a channel reopens, the queue that formed offshore during the closure arrives at once, and berth windows, pilots and tugs become the constraint. A closure of a few days can produce a backlog that takes longer than the closure itself to clear.

For now, those are contingencies. Forecast uncertainty for Rafael remains large several days out, and no change in port status had been announced for Corpus Christi as of Monday. Pilot operations and terminal loadings were continuing.

Gulfwater will report Coast Guard port condition changes for Corpus Christi and the anchorage count as they are announced.

item.title: Monthly high on the docks: Corpus Christi crude exports peak as anchorage waits persist
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Analysts put the port's share at about half of U.S. crude exports. On the water, that means tight berth windows going into the heart of hurricane season.
item.content:encoded:
Crude exports through the Port of Corpus Christi hit a monthly high, and analysts say the port now handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

Status, Thursday: port open to all traffic; tankers continue to wait at the offshore anchorage.

On the docks. A monthly high shows up as short gaps between ships at the crude berths, longer days for line handlers and tug crews, and little room to recover from a late cargo.

"It was a strong month, and it was a safe month," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Our customers are moving a great deal of crude and the channel is handling it."

The market view. "The share is the story," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, which tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "About half of the country's crude exports go out through one channel. When Corpus Christi is busy, the whole export system is busy."

Offshore. Waiting at the anchorage has been routine all summer, as Gulfwater has reported. The queue is a product of berth windows, not of any restriction in the channel.

The calendar. September is the peak of hurricane season, and forecasters expect above-normal activity for the rest of it. A port running this close to capacity has less slack to clear ships ahead of a storm, a point operators have been weighing since the outlook was updated.

Operator notes. Expect tight berth windows to continue. Confirm readiness times with agents before leaving the anchorage. Recreational traffic at the Port Aransas entrance will be heavy over the Labor Day weekend.

Gulfwater's explainers on the anchorage, on hurricane port conditions and on requests to remain in port are available to subscribers.

item.title: Explainer: staying at the berth in a hurricane, and what the Coast Guard asks first
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: At Port Condition X-Ray, ocean-going ships must plan to leave or get approval to stay. What goes into that request, and who carries the risk.
item.content:encoded:
Most heavy-weather plans for Corpus Christi end with the ship at sea. Some end with the ship still alongside. This explainer covers the second case.

The rule. When the Coast Guard sets Port Condition X-Ray, ocean-going vessels must plan to depart or request approval from the Captain of the Port to remain in port. No approval, no stay.

Why a ship would ask. Cargo is aboard and cannot be finished or discharged in time. The ship has a mechanical problem. Or the master and operator judge that a well-moored ship at a sheltered berth is safer than a late run for sea room through a crowded entrance.

What the request covers. The reason the ship cannot sail. The berth and the terminal's agreement. The mooring arrangement, including extra lines and how they will be tended. The ship's draft and ballast condition. Crew remaining aboard. Tug availability. Contact numbers that will work when shore power and cell service may not.

"A vessel that remains in port is still the master's responsibility and still the Captain of the Port's concern," said a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Approval is specific to that vessel, that berth and that forecast. It is not a standing permission."

Who carries the risk. A ship alongside faces surge, wind on the hull and strain on lines and fenders. The terminal's dock and loading arms sit next to it. A laden ship rides differently from a light one, and the mooring plan has to say which it will be.

Operator notes. Agree the plan with the terminal before the season, not at X-Ray. Decide in advance what cargo condition the ship will be left in and how cargo systems will be secured. Keep a written record of who approved what.

With loadings at a near-record pace, more ships are at the berth on any given day, and more operators may face the choice.

item.title: Above-normal outlook has tanker operators rereading heavy-weather plans
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Forecasters expect a busy rest of the season. With a full anchorage off Port Aransas, the practical question is how early is early enough.
item.content:encoded:
Forecasters now expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the hurricane season. For operators calling at Corpus Christi, where tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage, the outlook turns a paper exercise into a scheduling question.

Status, Wednesday: port open to all traffic. No tropical system threatens the Texas coast this week.

The problem in one paragraph. Ships at anchor must get under way and gain sea room before conditions build. Loaded ships at the berth must sail or obtain approval to remain. Inbound ships must slow down, divert or hold well offshore. All of them share one entrance at Port Aransas, and none of them can move faster than the pilots, tugs and daylight allow.

"Every plan says leave early," said a tanker agent who asked not to be named because he is not authorized to speak for his principals. "The argument is always about what early means when the cargo isn't finished."

That argument is commercial as much as nautical. A ship that sails with a part cargo, or leaves the line at the anchorage, gives up something. A ship that waits too long can lose the choice.

"Operators should not wait for a port condition to start planning," said a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "By the time X-Ray is set, the plan should already be in motion."

Operator notes. Decide now who has authority to stop cargo and order departure, and put the name in the plan. Agree with the terminal on how long a safe shutdown takes. Check that masters at the anchorage have current contact details for agents and for the Coast Guard. For ships that may ask to stay alongside, prepare the mooring plan before it is needed.

Gulfwater's explainer on hurricane port conditions ran Aug. 3.

item.title: One way in, one way out: how deep-draft transits are sequenced at Corpus Christi
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Pilots, tugs, terminals and the Coast Guard build the lineup every day. At a near-record loading pace there is little slack, and a short delay at one dock shows up offshore by evening.
item.content:encoded:
Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Saturday: open to all traffic. Crude loadings continue near record pace and the offshore anchorage remains busy.

The constraint. Every deep-draft ship bound for the Inner Harbor comes through the Port Aransas jetties and runs the length of the bay. Large loaded tankers move under pilot-set restrictions, which can include one-way traffic in narrow reaches, tug escort and limits tied to weather and visibility. The channel works more like a single-track railway than a highway.

Who builds the lineup. Pilots board at the sea buoy. Harbor tugs meet ships inside. Vessel agents, the pilots' dispatchers and the terminals trade berth windows and readiness times through the day, and the Coast Guard's vessel traffic service watches the result.

Why ships wait. A berth that is not clear, a cargo that finishes late, fog, or a missed daylight window each pushes the line back. At this pace, waiting at the anchorage is routine, not a sign of trouble.

"The lineup is a puzzle we solve every day," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "When loadings run this strong there isn't much slack, so a two-hour delay at one dock shows up offshore by evening."

What is coming. Late summer adds a military outload. A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation, and that cargo will take berth and channel time alongside the tanker schedule. Salinas said planning is on track. "We have done military moves before. It goes on the same board as everything else," he said.

Operator notes. Give agents honest arrival and readiness times; an optimistic estimate costs the whole line. Keep transponder data current. Expect recreational traffic at the entrance on weekends through Labor Day.

Gulfwater explained how the offshore anchorage works in July.

item.title: Corpus Christi anchorage stays busy as crude loadings run near record pace
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Export tankers continue to queue offshore east of Port Aransas for berths in the ship channel, which also serves the port's role as a strategic seaport for military cargo.
item.content:encoded:
Crude tankers continue to wait at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas as loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi run at a near-record pace, according to port activity and public AIS observations reviewed by Gulfwater.

The queue is not new. Waiting at anchor for a berth has become routine for export tankers calling at the Coastal Bend. Vessels arriving from the Gulf report to the anchorage, hold for a berth window and a pilot, then transit the entrance channel between the Port Aransas jetties and proceed up the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to terminals along the channel and the Inner Harbor.

Waiting times vary with berth schedules, weather and pilot and tug availability. The structural constraint is the channel itself: a single deep-draft route serving crude terminals, refineries, bulk docks and general cargo berths.

"Corpus Christi is running like a clock right now," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics who tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "The anchorage is the buffer. When everything's moving, nobody notices it."

The same channel carries military cargo. The Port of Corpus Christi is a designated strategic seaport, and a Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation. Military port movements at commercial strategic seaports are planned around commercial traffic, with berth and staging space coordinated in advance.

Hurricane season adds a variable that operators know well. When the Coast Guard tightens port conditions ahead of a tropical system, inbound traffic can be suspended, vessels at anchor commonly put to sea to ride out the weather, and oceangoing ships in port may be required to leave or to request permission to remain. The busiest weeks of the season are still ahead.

For now, the anchorage remains full and the channel open. Gulfwater will report changes in port status as the Coast Guard and the port announce them.

item.title: Summer traffic crowds the Port Aransas pass as tankers, ferries and charters share the entrance
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Deep-draft crude traffic and a strong tourist season are packing the entrance channel at Port Aransas this August.
item.content:encoded:
The entrance channel between the jetties at Port Aransas is carrying a heavy mix of traffic this summer, with crude tankers moving at a near-record export pace alongside ferries, charter boats and recreational vessels drawn by a strong tourist season.

Deep draft: Laden tankers outbound from Corpus Christi terminals and ballast tankers inbound from the offshore anchorage transit the pass with pilots aboard and tug escort as required. Large vessels have limited room to maneuver in the confined entrance and depend on other traffic to keep clear.

Ferries: The state-run ferries between Harbor Island and Port Aransas cross the ship channel just inside the pass, and summer demand keeps them running almost constantly. Ferry crossings are timed around deep-draft movements.

Small craft: Port Aransas businesses report a strong summer, with charters and bait shops busy. Charter boats, bay boats, kayaks and personal watercraft add to congestion around the jetties, particularly on weekend mornings and late afternoons. Anglers on the jetty rocks and boats anchored near the pass are a familiar sight to pilots bringing ships through.

Tugs and support: Harbor tugs, pilot boats and offshore supply vessels round out the picture. Tug crews working the entrance spend much of the summer threading between pleasure boats on their way to and from assignments.

Wind and visibility: Afternoon sea breezes and summer squalls can raise a steep chop in the pass and briefly cut visibility, adding to the workload for pilots and small-boat operators alike.

Rules of the road: Recreational boaters must not impede vessels that can navigate safely only within the channel, and federal navigation rules apply throughout the pass. The Coast Guard oversees channel traffic and can impose safety measures when conditions require.

Gulfwater will continue to track entrance-channel and anchorage conditions as the season moves toward its late-summer peak.

item.title: Freight forwarders book standby space for relief cargo as peak hurricane season nears
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Relief agencies are stocking warehouses and forwarders have signed standby contracts. At a port built around crude, the hard part after a storm is the channel, not the dock.
item.content:encoded:
Relief agencies along the Texas coast are stocking warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders have signed standby contracts to move relief cargo by sea if a storm hits, companies said this week.

What a standby contract is. A forwarder reserves the right to call on container slots, trucking and port handling at short notice. The cargo, typically water, tarps, generators and hygiene kits, is staged in advance so it can be loaded within days.

"You sign the paper in August so you are not making phone calls in September," said Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder. "The boxes are the easy part. The lane is the hard part. You need a ship, a berth and a truck on the other end, and after a storm all three are in short supply."

The port piece. Corpus Christi is built around liquid and bulk cargo. Crude is loading at a near-record pace, tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage, and berth time is tight. Relief cargo arriving after a storm would join the same queue for the same entrance.

"We plan for it every year," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Relief cargo gets attention when it is needed, and we work the sequence with the Coast Guard and the pilots. The limiting factor after a storm is usually the channel, not the dock."

Operator notes. Forwarders should confirm now which terminals can work containers and general cargo, and what handling gear is on site. After a hurricane, the entrance channel is surveyed before deep-draft traffic resumes, and the order of arrivals is set with the pilots under the Captain of the Port's direction. A ship that arrives first is not always the ship that berths first.

Akins said he hopes the contracts go unused. "The best year is the one where we never open the file," he said.

item.title: Explainer: Whiskey to Zulu, the Coast Guard's hurricane port conditions
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: No storm threatens Texas this week. With the peak of the season ahead and the anchorage busy, a plain reading of the four steps that close a port.
item.content:encoded:
Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Tuesday: open to all traffic. No tropical system threatens the Texas coast this week. The peak of hurricane season is ahead and the offshore anchorage is busy, which makes this the week to reread the plan.

The ladder. The Coast Guard Captain of the Port sets hurricane port conditions by the forecast time to gale-force winds. Whiskey: possible within 72 hours. X-Ray: within 48. Yankee: within 24. Zulu: within 12. Each step tightens what may move.

What changes. At Whiskey, operators review plans and report intentions. At X-Ray the port stays open, but ocean-going vessels must plan to depart or request approval to remain in port, and terminals begin winding down cargo work. At Yankee the port generally closes to inbound traffic. At Zulu the port is closed to all traffic.
