"The conditions are set by the forecast, and they are published," said a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Every operator calling at Corpus Christi should know today what the vessel will do at each step, and who on board and ashore makes that call."

Why Corpus Christi is tight. One entrance at Port Aransas serves the whole port. Departing tankers, ships leaving the anchorage, tows and local traffic all use it, and a departure queue takes hours to clear. Ships at anchor need sea room, which means getting under way early.

Operator notes. Build departure timelines back from X-Ray, not Yankee. Confirm bunkers, stores, crew and pilot availability before the first step. File any request to remain in port early, with a mooring plan. Keep agent and terminal contact lists current through crew changes.

After the storm. A port does not reopen on a timetable. The channel is surveyed and aids to navigation are checked before deep-draft traffic resumes, and the Captain of the Port lifts restrictions in stages.

Gulfwater will publish each change in port condition at Corpus Christi as it is issued.

item.title: Army outload to slot into Corpus Christi's crowded tanker schedule
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: A late-summer military movement will need berth time, pilots and tugs in a channel already running near-record crude volumes.
item.content:encoded:
The Port of Corpus Christi will handle a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment in late summer, Army and port officials said this week, adding a military outload to a channel already busy with near-record crude loadings.

Berths: Military equipment typically moves over general cargo or roll-on, roll-off berths rather than liquid bulk docks, so the outload does not compete directly with crude terminals for dock space. It does compete for channel time, pilots, tugs and line handlers.

Vessel: Unit equipment for overseas rotations commonly moves on government-controlled sealift ships with stern ramps and large internal vehicle decks. The Army has not identified the ship or released loading dates.

Staging: Before loading, unit equipment is typically marshaled in a staging area near the berth, checked against load plans and inspected for shipment. Helicopters usually move aboard with blades folded or removed and are secured on internal decks for the voyage.

Channel: Deep-draft tankers dominate traffic between the Port Aransas jetties and the Inner Harbor. A sealift transit is one more large-ship movement to sequence, with the additional coordination typical of military cargo.

Anchorage: Inbound tankers already wait offshore for berth windows. A port spokesperson said this month that anchorage traffic reflects demand. A single military movement is unlikely to change that picture much, but scheduling margins in a peak export summer are thin.

Strategic seaport: Corpus Christi is one of the commercial ports designated by the Defense Department to support military deployments, and it has moved Army cargo before. "We'll work the military cargo alongside our regular business," port spokesperson Javier Salinas said Wednesday.

Outlook: As with any late-summer schedule on the Texas coast, weather is the main variable. Gulfwater will report channel conditions and the outload as details become public.

item.title: Explainer: how the Corpus Christi offshore anchorage works when the docks are full
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Tankers waiting off Port Aransas are a routine part of a near-record export summer. Here is how the queue is managed.
item.content:encoded:
With crude export terminals on the Corpus Christi Ship Channel loading at a near-record pace, the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas has become a fixture on public vessel-tracking screens. On a typical day, tankers swing at anchor in the open Gulf, waiting for a berth.

Anchoring: Vessels that arrive without an open berth anchor in designated areas outside the entrance channel. Position, weather and holding ground all matter. In a strong onshore wind, masters may choose to drift or steam offshore rather than ride at anchor.

Sequencing: Terminals, ship agents and the port coordinate berth windows. When a berth clears, the next vessel is called in, picks up a pilot outside the jetties and transits the channel with tug assistance as required. The largest tankers face transit limits based on draft, beam, visibility and wind.

Why ships wait: Cargo readiness at the terminal, shore tank levels, documentation and inspections, and the departure of the vessel ahead all affect timing. Waits range from hours to days.

Who manages it: The Coast Guard sets port conditions and oversees traffic in the channel. Pilots, terminal operators and agents handle day-to-day movements. The port authority, which owns much of the dock infrastructure, describes the anchorage traffic as a normal sign of demand, as a port spokesperson told Gulfwater this month.

Mixed traffic: The anchorage area is also used by product tankers, bulk carriers and offshore supply vessels, and it sits near the approaches used by fishing and charter boats out of Port Aransas. AIS gives a reasonable picture of the larger ships present, although small craft are not required to broadcast and often do not.

Gulfwater will continue to report anchorage and channel conditions at Corpus Christi through the summer.

item.title: Explainer: what public AIS shows about a busy channel, and where it stops
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: With crude loadings near record pace and tankers waiting offshore, more readers are watching Corpus Christi on vessel-tracking sites. A guide to what that data is, and what it is not.
item.content:encoded:
Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Wednesday: open to all traffic, no restrictions. With crude loadings running near record pace and tankers routinely waiting at the offshore anchorage, more readers are watching the port through public vessel-tracking websites. This explainer covers what that data is and where it stops.

What it is. The Automatic Identification System is a shipboard radio transponder. It broadcasts a vessel's identity, position, course and speed to other ships and to shore stations. Commercial ships above set sizes must carry it. Receivers ashore and on satellites collect the broadcasts, and public websites replay them on a map.

What it is for. AIS was built for collision avoidance and traffic management, not for security. "It is a system where each ship reports on itself," said an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander who reviews public AIS data. "Most of the time that's fine, because most mariners want to be seen. But you are reading what the transponder says, not what a radar or a lookout saw."

What it shows well. The length of the queue at the anchorage, how long ships wait, which berths turn fastest and when traffic bunches at the Port Aransas entrance. Operators use the same picture to plan arrivals.

Where it stops. Coverage has gaps. A transponder can be switched off, can fail, or can be loaded with wrong details. Small craft often carry none. The analyst said the useful habit is comparison. "One position report tells you very little. A track that matches the ship's schedule, its speed and its last port tells you a lot. When those things stop agreeing, that is when I look twice," he said.

Operator notes. Check that static data, including name, call sign and dimensions, is entered correctly after yard periods and crew changes. Report transponder faults to the Coast Guard's vessel traffic service before arrival. Do not navigate from a public website.

Gulfwater uses public AIS in its port coverage and says so when it does.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude loadings run near record pace; offshore anchorage stays busy
item.dc:creator: Henrik Aalto
item.description: Export terminals on the Corpus Christi Ship Channel are loading tankers at one of their fastest clips on record, and vessels waiting for berths remain a routine sight off Port Aransas.
item.content:encoded:
Crude oil loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi are running at a near-record pace this summer. Export terminals along the ship channel are working a steady rotation of tankers, and inbound vessels routinely hold at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas until berths clear.

The pattern is familiar to anyone watching public AIS data off the Coastal Bend. Laden and ballast tankers alternate through the entrance channel between the Port Aransas jetties, take a pilot and transit the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to terminals at Ingleside and along the Inner Harbor. Vessels without a confirmed berth window anchor offshore and wait.

"Our terminals are busy, the channel is open and the ships keep coming," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Seeing tankers at the anchorage is a sign of demand. That's what a working export port looks like."

Anchorage time is driven by several factors: berth availability, cargo readiness at the terminal, pilot and tug scheduling, and the transit restrictions that apply to the largest ships in the channel. Depending on the queue, a tanker can wait hours or several days.

Crude reaches the terminals by pipeline from West Texas production fields. The export trade has reshaped the port, adding storage tanks, dock space and a deeper channel to handle larger ships.

The practical effect of the pace is tighter scheduling. With berths in steady use, a vessel that arrives late for its window, or a terminal that falls behind on cargo, can push the next ship back into the anchorage queue.

For mariners, the result is a busier pass. Ferries crossing to Port Aransas, recreational boats, offshore supply vessels and harbor tugs share the entrance with deep-draft tankers, and summer adds charter and pleasure traffic to the mix.

Gulfwater will continue to track anchorage conditions and channel traffic at Corpus Christi through the summer.
